articles.title: Americast - Will Trump’s $5,000 offer convince US voters? - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Trump made the pledge at the Republicans’ first ever midterm convention.
articles.body: President Trump made the pledge at the Republicans' first ever midterm convention, promising every adult American a $5,000 payment if his party wins both chambers of Congress in November. Sarah, who was in the arena in Dallas watching Trump’s speech, and Justin look at whether this is a serious policy or a desperate measure. The payment would cost over a trillion dollars, no detail has been given on how it would work, and federal law restricts payments made in connection with how people vote. JD Vance has suggested it could be paid for by revenue raised from trade tariffs. Trump told supporters to pretend he was on the ballot himself, and said he would campaign in every close race. But with his approval ratings at historic lows, an unpopular war with Iran, and some Republicans on the ballot this year choosing to stay away from the convention, is he now more of a hindrance than a help to his own party? And a year on from the killing of Charlie Kirk, Justin and Sarah discuss his legacy on the American right, and ask whether anyone has emerged to take his place. articles.title: Pipoca em Cena: alunos de Manaus lançam curtas sobre meio ambiente | G1
articles.standfirst: Produções abordam temas ligados ao meio ambiente e podem ser assistidas no canal da Fundação Rede Amazônica no YouTube.
articles.summary: O projeto Pipoca em Cena disponibiliza no YouTube curtas-metragens sobre o meio ambiente produzidos por alunos de uma escola pública de Manaus.
articles.body:
Pipoca em Cena: curtas produzidos por alunos da Zona Oeste de Manaus chegam ao público — Foto: Foto: João Paulo Oliveira/Rede Amazônica

Os curtas-metragens produzidos por alunos da Escola Estadual Cívico-Militar Fueth Paulo Mourão, localizada no bairro São Jorge, na Zona Oeste de Manaus , já podem ser assistidos pelo público. As produções fazem parte da 12ª edição do Pipoca em Cena, iniciativa da Fundação Rede Amazônica que utiliza o audiovisual como ferramenta de formação, expressão artística e protagonismo juvenil.

Entre as histórias produzidas pelos alunos está uma que aborda questões relacionadas à poluição e ao descarte inadequado de resíduos. A produção acompanha uma menina que sonha com uma fada e, ao longo da narrativa, se depara com situações ligadas ao cuidado com o meio ambiente.

Durante o projeto, os participantes tiveram contato com diferentes etapas da produção audiovisual, desde a construção das histórias até as gravações e a edição. Agora, os filmes produzidos pela turma podem ser conferidos pelo público no canal da Fundação Rede Amazônica .

Para Anderson Mendes, oficineiro e gerente de Conteúdo da Fundação Rede Amazônica, a experiência também amplia as possibilidades de expressão dos participantes por meio do audiovisual.

“A proposta é que eles entendam que o audiovisual também pode ser uma forma de contar histórias sobre o lugar onde vivem e discutir questões que fazem parte do cotidiano deles.”

A publicação dos curtas permite que as produções sejam acessadas além do ambiente escolar e conhecidas por outras pessoas. Os filmes integram o conjunto de 20 produções realizadas nesta edição do Pipoca em Cena.

O Pipoca em Cena é uma iniciativa da Fundação Rede Amazônica que utiliza o audiovisual como ferramenta de formação, expressão artística e protagonismo juvenil. Nesta 12ª edição, cerca de cem estudantes de duas escolas públicas de Manaus participam das atividades e produzem 20 curtas-metragens com histórias relacionadas ao meio ambiente e à sustentabilidade.

A programação reúne oficinas de produção audiovisual, experiências culturais, exibição dos filmes produzidos pelos alunos e atividades de encerramento. O projeto conta com apoio da Eucatur Urbano e da Globo Filmes.

articles.title: VÍDEO: Caseiro atravessa rio de trator durante período de estiagem | G1
articles.standfirst: Travessia no Rio Muru foi feita por Everton Oliveira de 21 anos, em Tarauacá, na última quarta-feira (9). Trajeto faz parte da rotina do caseiro e dá acesso até a fazenda onde trabalha.
articles.summary: Travessia no Rio Muru foi feita por Everton Oliveira de 21 anos, em Tarauacá, na última quarta (9). Trajeto faz parte da rotina do caseiro e dá acesso até fazenda onde trabalha.
articles.body:
O caseiro Everton Oliveira de 21 anos, atravessou de trator um trecho do Rio Muru, em Tarauacá , no interior do Acre, quando ia para a fazenda que trabalha na última quarta-feira (9) e registrou o momento.

No vídeo, ele aparece dirigindo o trator pela água, enquanto o amigo, que estava montado em um cavalo, segue à frente. O percurso até a outra margem levou mais de três minutos. ( Veja vídeo acima )

Segundo a Defesa Civil Municipal, o manancial marca 3,63 metros na manhã desta sexta (11), no entanto, há percursos em que o manancial está mais baixo e, por isso, é possível a travessia.

Ao g1 , Everton contou que a travessia faz parte da rotina de acesso à fazenda em que trabalha e que, todos os anos, espera o nível do rio baixar para conseguir passar com o trator.

Ele costuma sair da cidade pelo ramal e atravessar o manancial em um ponto que fica próximo à propriedade.

Everton atravessa de trator um trecho do Rio Muru, em Tarauacá, para chegar até a fazenda em que trabalha — Foto: Reprodução

“Todo ano a gente espera o rio dar uma baixada para passar com o trator. Como já deu uma baixada, a gente conseguiu essa semana”, contou.

A passagem, porém, ainda não é suficiente para transportar cargas maiores até a fazenda. De acordo com ele, quando o rio fica mais seco, eles também aproveitam para levar ração e sacas de sal para os animais usando uma carroça.

“Quando ele seca mais a gente desce com a carroça e embarca as coisas. Mas ainda não está num período bom de fazer a travessia com esses produtos porque está meio fundo”, afirmou.

Everton explicou também que o nível do Muru não baixa da mesma forma todos os anos. Há períodos em que o rio seca bastante, mas também anos em que a água não recua tanto.

Everton atravessa de trator um trecho do Rio Muru, em Tarauacá, para chegar até a fazenda em que trabalha — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

“Não é tão comum ficar baixo assim, porque tem ano que não baixa totalmente assim, mas tem épocas que seca bastante, então depende muito. Alguns trechos são mais secos que outros”, disse.

Ainda de acordo com Everton, quando o rio está cheio e a passagem por dentro da água não é possível, a alternativa é usar embarcação ou uma balsa.

Segundo o coordenador da Defesa Civil de Tarauacá, Leandro Simões, o município tem registrado chuvas rápidas e curtas. Para esta sexta por exemplo, a previsão indicada pelo órgão era de 38% de possibilidade de chuva.

''A região passa por um período de estiagem e a previsão é de que o nível do rio ainda possa baixar um pouco mais. Ainda não atingimos o pico do verão'', explicou.

Apesar da estiagem, o órgão informou que os números de queimadas estão dentro da média esperada para o período e que não há, no momento, grandes alertas relacionados aos focos de incêndio.

O calor deve continuar sendo um dos principais destaques dos próximos meses em diferentes regiões do país. Uma análise do Centro Nacional de Monitoramento e Alertas de Desastres Naturais (Cemaden) aponta possibilidade de pelo menos seis ondas de calor no Brasil nos próximos meses.

O número pode ser ainda maior, já que, durante o último El Niño, foram registradas nove ondas de calor . O fenômeno é diferente de um dia isoladamente quente.

Para ser considerada uma onda de calor, a situação precisa persistir por pelo menos três dias consecutivos, com temperaturas máximas e mínimas excepcionalmente acima do normal.

A análise considera um histórico de 47 anos de registros de temperatura e períodos de ocorrência do El Niño. A previsão indica a possibilidade de um episódio de forte intensidade, com efeitos diferentes entre as regiões do país, mas com um ponto em comum: a persistência de temperaturas elevadas.

articles.title: Leilão de veículos no Piauí: motos têm lances a partir de R$ 150 | G1
articles.standfirst: Poderão participar pessoas físicas inscritas no Cadastro de Pessoas Físicas (CPF) e pessoas jurídicas inscritas no Cadastro Nacional da Pessoa Jurídica (CNPJ).
articles.summary: O leilão de veículos no Piauí oferece 76 lotes para pessoas físicas e jurídicas com lances iniciais de R$ 150 para motos e R$ 2 mil para carros.
articles.body:
Moto e carro no leilão (Imagens ilustrativas) — Foto: Divulgação/Lance Certo Leilões

O Governo do Estado do Piauí vai realizar, no dia 21 de setembro, um leilão virtual de bens considerados inservíveis para a administração pública. O certame ocorrerá das 9h às 17h e contará com 76 lotes.

🔍Bens inservíveis são veículos, móveis e equipamentos que não têm mais utilidade para a administração pública, mas ainda podem ser reaproveitados.

Do total de lotes disponíveis, 43 são veículos e 33 reúnem equipamentos de informática, móveis e outros materiais permanentes. Entre os veículos disponíveis, há carros com lances iniciais a partir de R$ 2 mil e motocicletas com lances a partir de R$ 150.

Poderão participar pessoas físicas inscritas no Cadastro de Pessoas Físicas (CPF) e pessoas jurídicas inscritas no Cadastro Nacional da Pessoa Jurídica (CNPJ).

Para participar do leilão, os interessados deverão realizar cadastro prévio na plataforma responsável pelo certame . Será necessário informar os dados solicitados, anexar documento oficial com foto, comprovante de endereço e um termo de adesão assinado.

As imagens dos bens, as condições de participação e as demais informações sobre o procedimento estão disponíveis na plataforma do leilão.

O edital também pode ser consultado no site e reúne a descrição dos lotes, as regras de participação e as demais condições do certame.

articles.title: Alckmin defende investigação do caso Master e quebra de sigilo de todos os envolvidos: ‘Inclusive do Dark Horse’ | G1
articles.standfirst: Vice-presidente participou de ato político em Pindamonhangaba nesta sexta-feira (11) ao lado de Fernando Haddad e Marina Silva e também destacou obras na Via Dutra e investimentos no Vale do Paraíba.
articles.summary: Vice-presidente participou de ato político em Pindamonhangaba nesta sexta-feira (11) ao lado de Fernando Haddad e Marina Silva e também destacou obras na Via Dutra e investimentos no Vale do Paraíba.
articles.body:
O vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin (PSB), novamente candidato a vice, defendeu nesta sexta-feira (11) a investigação do caso Master e a quebra do sigilo de todos os envolvidos, inclusive de quem estiver relacionado ao filme “Dark Horse”.

A fala de Alckmin aconteceu durante um ato político no Sindicato dos Metalúrgicos de Pindamonhangaba, no interior de São Paulo. O vice-presidente classificou o episódio como o “golpe do Master”.

“Quem quer dar golpe, o máximo que fez foi o golpe do Master, que precisa ser investigado, investigado. Nós queremos é que quebre o sigilo de todos os envolvidos. Inclusive do Dark Horse. Melhor é a luz do sol, é respeito. O que a sociedade quer é a verdade”, disse.

🔍 “Dark Horse” é um filme sobre a vida do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro. A produção é alvo de uma investigação da Polícia Federal que apura suspeitas relacionadas ao financiamento da obra. Já o caso Master envolve investigações da PF relacionadas ao Banco Master e ao ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro. Nesta sexta-feira, a Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) pediu a retirada do sigilo de todos os documentos do caso.

Geraldo Alckmin (PSB) participa de ato político em Pindamonhangaba, no interior de São Paulo — Foto: Reprodução/Rede Vanguarda

Alckmin também comparou a postura do governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) com a do governo anterior, de Jair Bolsonaro, ao falar sobre investigações envolvendo familiares de autoridades.

“E aí vejam o que é espírito republicano, da 'res pública'. Espírito republicano. No governo anterior teve denúncia contra familiar, quatro delegados gerais foram demitidos pelo governo. O ministro foi demitido para esconder tudo. No governo do presidente Lula, transparência total”, afirmou.

Alckmin, o candidato ao governo de São Paulo Fernando Haddad (PT) e a candidata ao Senado Marina Silva (Rede) participaram do ato político no Sindicato dos Metalúrgicos de Pindamonhangaba na tarde desta sexta-feira (11).

Durante o evento, Alckmin destacou as obras de terceira e quarta faixas da Via Dutra entre São José dos Campos e Aparecida e o projeto de um caminho seguro para romeiros entre Guarulhos e Aparecida.

Segundo ele, as intervenções representam cerca de R$ 1 bilhão em investimentos adicionais previstos no contrato de concessão da rodovia.

Haddad defendeu a reindustrialização, a educação profissional e o uso de inteligência artificial na gestão pública. Marina Silva destacou a vulnerabilidade do Vale do Paraíba a eventos climáticos extremos e defendeu investimentos em ciência, tecnologia, inovação e turismo.

Mais cedo, pela manhã, Alckmin e Haddad conversaram de forma particular com o arcebispo de Aparecida, Dom Mário Antônio da Silva, empossado em maio deste ano. Haddad também concedeu entrevista a uma rádio antes do ato político.

articles.title: Disputa pela final da Copa vira polêmica entre Marrocos e Espanha | G1
articles.standfirst: Federações de futebol dos dois países querem receber o último jogo do torneio. Briga casou divisão política no Marrocos.
articles.summary: Federações de futebol dos dois países querem receber o último jogo do torneio. Briga casou divisão política no Marrocos.
articles.body:
A disputa para decidir onde será realizada a final da Copa do Mundo de 2030 ganhou força nesta sexta-feira (11), depois que o primeiro-ministro do Marrocos pediu que o presidente da federação de futebol do país pare de fazer promessas sobre a sede da decisão. A Espanha também entrou na disputa.

A Fifa ainda não anunciou qual dos três países que vão receber a competição — Espanha, Portugal ou Marrocos — sediará a final. A organização disse que o anúncio será feito em um momento oportuno.

O primeiro-ministro marroquino, Aziz Akhannouch, criticou o presidente da Federação Real Marroquina de Futebol (RMFF), Fouzi Lekjaa, que havia declarado, durante um evento de um partido político, que Casablanca teria a "honra" de receber a decisão.

"Não se ofereçam para sediar a grande final no Marrocos enquanto ainda não discutimos o assunto com nossos aliados, Espanha e Portugal. Deveria haver um pouco de respeito, irmãos", disse Akhannouch.

"Parem de usar promessas eleitorais para nos tirar o chão. Essas são questões de grande importância. Decidir onde a final será realizada é uma questão de grande peso."

Taça da Copa do Mundo 2026 que será erguida neste domingo. — Foto: JUAN MABROMATA/AFP

O presidente da Federação Espanhola de Futebol (RFEF), Rafael Louzán, também rejeitou a declaração do dirigente marroquino e defendeu que a final seja realizada na Espanha.

Louzán classificou a promessa de Lekjaa como um "slogan eleitoral" e afirmou que o país tem motivos para receber a decisão, entre eles o fato de ser o atual campeão mundial.

"Embora nenhuma decisão tenha sido tomada [pela Fifa], acredito que a Espanha seja o lugar certo, pois não poderia ser de outra forma. Como vocês sabem, atualmente somos campeões mundiais", disse Louzán à rádio Cadena SER.

"Acredito que a capacidade organizacional da Espanha para grandes eventos é inquestionável e é por isso que a realidade dita que a grande final não pode e não deve ser realizada em nenhum outro lugar que não seja a Espanha."

articles.title: Após alagamentos, dez famílias são retiradas de casa e acolhidas em abrigo em Sumaré | G1
articles.standfirst: Temporal desta sexta-feira afetou aproximadamente 100 residências na cidade; prefeitura mobilizou estrutura de assistência no CIE do Jardim Bordon.
articles.summary: Temporal desta sexta-feira afetou aproximadamente 100 residências na cidade; prefeitura mobilizou estrutura de assistência no CIE do Jardim Bordon.
articles.body:
Dez famílias precisaram deixar suas casas em razão dos alagamentos provocados pelo temporal que atingiu Sumaré (SP) nesta sexta-feira (11).

Segundo a prefeitura, as famílias foram acolhiadas no CIE (Centro Integrado de Esportes) do Jardim Bordon, que foi disponibilizado como espaço de abrigo e atendimento emergencial.

"As equipes municipais estão mobilizadas para garantir às famílias acolhimento, segurança, alimentação e assistência durante o período em que permanecerem no local", informou, em nota.

Um dos locais mais atingidos foi na Rua Claudemir Eugenio, na Vila Diva. Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, ao menos sete pessoas precisaram ser socorridas com o uso de um barco .

A prefeitura informou que áreas próximas também foram atingidas. Entre os pontos afetados informados pela Defesa Civil estão:

Também houve registros de alagamentos na Vila Yolanda Costa e Silva, Jardim Dulce, Jardim Santa Teresinha e Jardim Paulistano.

Na Vila Menuzzo, na região central, o pluviômetro registrou 99 mm de chuva em 24 horas . Em Nova Veneza, foram 56 mm no mesmo período.

Sumaré tem 100 casas atingidas e resgates de barco após temporal — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

A previsão indica chuva intensa durante a noite desta sexta-feira, com possibilidade de continuidade ao longo de toda a madrugada de sábado (12).

A orientação da Defesa Civil é para que a população:

não tente atravessar trechos com acúmulo de água; e

procure locais seguros durante períodos de chuva intensa.

articles.title: Grupo Mandic abre inscrições para Vestibular em Medicina 2027 | G1
articles.standfirst: Inscrições para o processo seletivo, com 380 vagas em Campinas, Araras, Limeira e Arcoverde (PE), vão até 9/10/2026. Aulas começam em 1º de fevereiro de 2027.
articles.summary: Inscrições para o processo seletivo, com 380 vagas em Campinas, Araras, Limeira e Arcoverde (PE), vão até 9/10/2026. Aulas começam em 1º de fevereiro de 2027.
articles.body:
Grupo Mandic abre inscrições para Vestibular em Medicina 2027 — Foto: Crédito: Divulgação

O Grupo Mandic está com inscrições abertas para o Vestibular Unificado em Medicina, com vagas para ingresso no primeiro semestre de 2027 nas unidades de Campinas, Araras, Limeira, no estado de São Paulo (SP), e na Faculdade de Medicina do Sertão, em Arcoverde (PE). Ao todo, serão disponibilizadas 380 vagas. As provas serão realizadas em duas modalidades: presencial e on-line, nos dias 17/10/2026 para a Faculdade de Medicina do Sertão, em Arcoverde (PE) e no dia 18/10/2026, na Mandic de Campinas (SP), Araras (SP) e Limeira (SP). O processo seletivo é unificado, cabendo ao candidato escolher a unidade de sua preferência e a modalidade da prova no ato da inscrição. A prova on-line acontecerá no dia 21/10/2026.

Em Campinas, são 174 vagas disponíveis, sendo: 87 para prova presencial e 87 para a prova on-line.

Na unidade de Araras, são oferecidas 82 vagas, sendo 41 para a prova presencial e 41 para os que vão concorrer à prova on-line. Em Limeira, a Mandic oferece 36 vagas, sendo 18 para a prova presencial e 18 para a prova on-line.

Para a Faculdade de Medicina do Sertão (FMS), em Arcoverde, são 88 vagas, sendo 41 para a prova presencial e 41 para a prova on-line.

articles.title: Shashi Tharoor answers Chidambaram’s questions on Brics benefits for India; BJP takes digs
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Shashi Tharoor not being in sync with his Congress colleagues is no longer news. Especially, if the issue in question pertains to the globa.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Shashi Tharoor not being in sync with his Congress colleagues is no longer news. Especially, if the issue in question pertains to the global stage. So, when senior Congress leader Chidambaram questioned the benefits of Brics for India, Tharoor had an answer. As expected, the answer triggered another round of Tharoor vs Congress debate that overshadowed the BJP broadside against Chidambaram.On Wednesday, Chidambaram questioned the tangible benefits India has gained from recent Brics summits, and said he had not seen any significant outcomes from the last two or three meetings.“I don't know how many presidents and how many prime ministers are coming. I don't think the last two or three Brics summits have resulted in tangible benefits or tangible results,” Chidambaram stated. “In fact, we are part of Brics, we are part of SCO, we are part of G20, and we are part of QUAD. What benefits are we getting out of that? I can't see. In the last two or three summits, I didn't see any benefits. Earlier, the Brics summits resulted in some tangible benefits,” he added.Chidambaram’s remarks opened the floodgates for counter-attacks from the ruling party. The BJP leaders launched a broadside against Chidambaram and the Congress. What followed was a barrage of attacks ranging from "Dimagi Naxal", "Naraz Fufas in pain", "FOMO", "indigestion", "bitten by bug" to questions on what Congress had gained in diplomacy since Independence"Is diplomacy to be seen as a transaction like the Congress Party is projecting? What have I done for you? What will you do for me? Kind of an approach. What is the so-called tangible result?" BJP leader Nalin Kohli wondered.Kohli then questioned the Congress party's own diplomatic record from Independence until 2014. "If we talk of tangible results, we can question what the Congress Party's entire approach from 1947 right up to 2014 was on diplomacy, including Sharm El Sheikh and projecting Pakistan as literally a victim of terror when it is the perpetrator of terror," he stated.Tharoor joins debateTharoor then joined the debate and said India holding Brics was a matter of prestige. "Having a dozen heads of state and government, not only members of Brics but also some observers coming at presidential and prime ministerial level, is a matter of great prestige for us. It shows a certain diplomatic convening power, which has value in and of itself on the global stage," Tharoor said.The Congress MP maintained that the Brics Summit is providing an important platform for the Global South."This grouping, the 11 Brics countries, represents a majority of the world's population and 41 per cent of global GDP. It's not a small matter; it's something that has to be taken very seriously by the rest of the world. Secondly, of course, having a dozen heads of state and government, not only members of BRICS but also some observers coming at the presidential and prime ministerial level, this is a matter of great prestige for us," the Congress MP from Thiruvananthapuram said.Latching onto Tharoor’s remarks, Nalin Kohli said: “One has noted Dr Shashi Tharoor's statement, and anyone who understands diplomacy would see great value in the BRICS summit.”BJP leader Pradeep Bhandari also used Tharoor’s remarks to take digs at the Congress and allege that some party leaders were opposing Brics on the instructions of Rahul Gandhi.“Congress exposes Congress! Congress MP Shashi Tharoor says-" BRICS happening in India is a matter of huge prestige for Bharat." Congress MP exposes "Naraz Fufa" of Congress who were opposing BRICS on instructions of Rahul Gandhi!” Pradeep Bhandari said in a post on X.Tharoor has had frosty ties with the Congress over his “independent views” on a range of issues. In the last two years, Tharoor has often made the Congress duck for cover as the BJP has cited his views to school the grand-old-party. The Thiruvananthapuram MP has made several remarks over a wide range of issues - from lessons in nationalism to global diplomacy to the Emergency to Covid-19 vaccine distribution abroad - that have brought more cheers to the BJP than his own party, the Congress.Tharoor vs CongressIt all started with Tharoor's surprise "out-of-turn" praise for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s US trip after Donald Trump took oath as president for a second term.Tharoor then acknowledged key achievements from PM Modi’s visit, particularly on trade negotiations and defence cooperation. He welcomed the trade deal discussions and expressed optimism over India’s diplomatic engagements.The Congress immediately issued a clarification, which said that individual opinions do not reflect the party’s official stance. But Tharoor defended his remarks and said: “When someone in the government does the right thing, it should be recognised, irrespective of who's in power. For 16 years, I have been in politics. My attitude has been that when somebody in the government, whether it’s our government or some other party’s government, does the right thing or does something well, one should acknowledge and praise it, and when they do something badly, one should criticise it. If I were to praise all the time, no one would take me seriously. If I were to criticise all the time, no one would take me seriously either… There’s got to be some give and take in democracy.”After the Pahalgam terror attack and Centre's Operation Sindoor, Tharoor made several remarks that were at variance with the official stand taken by the Congress.Tharoor was picked up to lead a multi-party parliamentary delegation to represent India globally following Operation Sindoor. Later, writing for The Hindu, Tharoor praised Modi’s "energy, dynamism, and willingness to engage" as a major asset for India on the global stage. He described Modi’s multi-alignment strategy as a key pillar in projecting India's voice globally.At one stage, Tharoor said Modi’s foreign policy was remarkable as the Prime Minister was maintaining excellent relations with Russia while simultaneously pursuing strategic relations with the USA. Modi has raised Bharat as a powerful and independent force and has put forward a policy of “multi-alignment”.In May last year, during the inauguration of the Vizhinjam International Seaport in Thiruvananthapuram, Prime Minister Modi acknowledged the presence of Tharoor on stage and remarked that it would give "sleepless nights" to many in the opposition INDIA bloc.Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi held a meeting with Tharoor in January this year ahead of assembly elections in Kerala and tried to sort out the differences and project a unified picture.Tharoor has all along defended his remarks and has claimed that his stand on several international issues was "pro-India, and not pro-BJP," stressing that national interest transcends party lines.Clearly, for Shashi Tharoor, his remarks on Brics are par for the course. It is the Congress that has to decide - how to handle the independent views of its MP from Thiruvananthapuram.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US diplomacy under fire as Russia escalates attacks on Ukrainian officials
articles.summary: The Witkoff-Kushner visit to Moscow was immediately followed by Russian attacks on Kyiv.
articles.body:
United States envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been seen as embarrassing and amateurish after their latest attempt to secure a ceasefire in Russia’s war in Ukraine, suggesting that European patience with the US administration of Donald Trump is running out.

“Jared Kushner’s incompetence was on full display this weekend,” wrote Slate magazine. “The Witkoff-Kushner circus act is an embarrassment,” said the Daily Telegraph, while the Financial Times titled its story, “Kushner and Witkoff’s blind amateurism.”

Washington has pursued negotiations without its European allies since US President Donald Trump cut off military aid to Ukraine and agreed to meet with Putin last year.

Witkoff caused outrage after he openly flattered Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“When we retire, we’ll have all these incredible stories and incredible memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all,” he told Putin.

Ukraine stopped firing missiles and drones at Moscow between September 5 and 7 to enable the US envoys aircraft to fly safely between the capitals.

Russia also paused attacks as they visited Kyiv.

“Please come more often, so that our people have the chance to live normally,” Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy joked at a media conference with them.

But as soon as Witkoff and Kushner left, Russia showered drones and missiles on Kyiv killing at least four civilians on September 8 and 9.

Russia has shown little sign that it is ready for a deal. Putin’s diplomatic aide, Valery Ushakov, told the US envoys that Moscow was committed to achieving all its goals in Ukraine.

“Russia intends to achieve the goals of the special military operation,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov asserted on September 8.

“Of course, we’re all interested in ending the conflict as quickly as possible. Moreover, it must end on our terms, in order to prevent the possibility of it recurring in the future or spreading into a global conflict,” former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev told Vedomosti newspaper two days later. “Nuclear weapons can be used in certain circumstances. This isn’t a scare tactic,” he warned.

Zelenskyy has insisted that only leverage on the battlefield will force Moscow to negotiate.

“Without a strong position on the ground, there will only be ultimatums,” Zelenskyy said this week.

Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Kyiv on the fourth anniversary of Ukraine’s Kharkiv offensive, which reclaimed 11,500sq km (4,440 square miles) of northern Ukrainian territory from Russian occupation, including more than 500 settlements.

Shortly after that, Russian forces withdrew from roughly 8,000sq km (3,100 square miles) of territory it had occupied on the right bank of the Dnipro River in the southern region of Kherson, deeming it to be indefensible.

Both actions, along with Russia previously lifting sieges on Kyiv, Sumy and Chernihiv, reduced the Russian occupation from more than a quarter of Ukrainian territory to less than a fifth.

Since then, Russia has made only marginal gains for mounting losses.

Ukraine’s military leadership said that since the beginning of the war, Russia has suffered 1.5m losses of personnel – both soldiers killed or incapacitated.

This year, Russia has again suffered setbacks, notably during the Oleksandrivka counteroffensive, which reclaimed 745sq km (290 square miles) in the eastern and southern Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions.

Russia has appeared to have escalated its targeting of Ukrainian officials in recent days.

On September 4, a drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s internal security service, the SBU. “The drone was deliberately directed at the office of the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine, Oleksandr Poklad,” said the SBU.

Ukrainian defence adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said it was a jet-powered Geran-4 Russian drone – one of two launched from the occupied eastern Donetsk region and sent in tandem towards Kyiv.

One of the SBU’s main tasks is to arrest Russian agents guiding enemy artillery and drone strikes on Ukrainian soil. Beskrestnov believed an agent within 5km (3 miles) of SBU headquarters directed the drone intended for Poklad in its final stages.

“I instructed Poklad to respond appropriately, significantly and, if possible, in kind,” said Zelenskyy, later adding that “the geographical areas for the response have been determined”.

On September 8, Russia also came close to blowing up Zelenskyy’s plane as it waited on the tarmac the Moldovan capital, Chisinau.

The plane was carrying Zelenskyy, his wife Olena and Moldovan premier Maia Sandu to Oslo for the funeral of King Harald V.

Norwegian premier Jonas Gahr Store said the plane came close to being hit.

Both incidents came after Zelenskyy warned airlines on September 1 that “Russian airspace is becoming completely dangerous” and was “in effect closing” due to Ukrainian long-range drone operations.

Ukraine continued its long-range operations during the past week, targeting Russian oil and military infrastructure.

Between September 4 and 10, Ukraine struck at least seven refineries and gas condensate processing plants, two of them at an unprecedented 3,000km (1,860 miles) range from its border – the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky gas condensate plants, are beyond the Ural Mountains in the Siberian Arctic region of Yamalia.

Closer to home, Ukraine also struck the military airfield at Rostov-on-Don and the Russian port of Makhachkala on the Caspian Sea.

The Ukrainian military said they were “used to supply military personnel in both directions: components and attack UAVs of the Shahed type from Iran to the Russian Federation, [and] explosives, components for drones and ammunition from the Russian Federation to Iran”.

Ukraine sees the attacks as effective, since Russia’s finance ministry reported a $67.9bn deficit for the first eight months of the war. That is one-and-a-half times its deficit during the same period last year and far beyond the $44.5bn deficit budgeted for in all of 2026.

The ministry cited rising expenditures and falling revenues from oil and gas.

Those revenues were 16 percent lower than the first eight months of 2025, at just under $58bn, said Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service.

The expenditures are almost certainly military. The Intelligence Service assessed that Russia spent a record $126.7bn on defence in the first half of this year. That is 30 percent higher than in the same period of last year, 65 percent higher than in the first half of 2024 and 145 percent higher than in the corresponding period of 2023.

articles.title: Family of off-duty FDNY firefighter retraces steps as Tunnel to Towers mission continues on 9/11 anniversary
articles.summary: Tunnel to Towers Foundation chairman and CEO Frank Siller and relatives retraced the steps of his late brother Stephen Siller, a firefighter who died responding to the 9/11 attack.
articles.body: Tunnel to Towers Foundation Chairman and CEO Frank Siller and family members honored his late brother Stephen Siller — a heroic 34-year-old husband, father, and firefighter who, after hearing about the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attack, loaded himself down with gear, and traversed through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel on foot heading to the Twin Towers, and ultimately giving his life — by retracing the man's steps on Friday as Americans marked the grim 25th anniversary of the heinous attacks. "Together, they carried Stephen’s memory, his legacy, and the promise that his sacrifice – like so many others – would Never Be Forgotten," Tunnel to Towers noted in a press release. The charity transported a steel beam from one of the Twin Towers around the U.S. for several months, with their "Steel Across America" tour finally culminating with the Siller family's trek through the tunnel today. AMERICA MARKS 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS "This morning’s walk through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel was part of the conclusion of Steel Across America, a journey that began four-and-a-half months ago and carried a 21-foot, 16,900-pound World Trade Center steel beam more than 10,500 miles through nearly 40 stops across the country and back, stopping in more than 21 states," the organization noted. "For over four months, the steel has been a gathering place for communities to remember the events of September 11th, to honor first responders and veterans, and to ensure that a new generation understands the significance of what happened 25 years ago." Stephen Siller Jr., who was just 9 months old when his father died, according to Frank Siller, said during a Friday morning appearance on "Fox & Friends," "The Tunnel to Towers foundation has given my family so much, through the loss of my father, through the work we're doing to keep his memory alive. Every day we have events across the country. Every day we're helping somebody in his name. That is such a beautiful, beautiful gift," he noted. FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE Stephen Siller went to help respond to the 9/11 attacks after having already worked an overnight shift with the New York City Fire Department, according to Tunnel to Towers. "On the morning of September 11, 2001, Stephen had just completed his overnight shift as an FDNY firefighter and was going to play golf with his brothers when he heard about the attacks on the World Trade Center on his personal scanner. He turned his car around and headed toward Manhattan to help. When he found that his unit had already responded and that the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel closed to traffic, he strapped 60 pounds of firefighting gear to his back and ran through the tunnel on foot toward the Twin Towers. Stephen, like so many others that day, never came home," the organization noted. FAMILY OF 9/11 HERO TO RETRACE HIS STEPS IN FINAL TUNNEL TO TOWERS STOP CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Born from the tragedy of 9/11, the Tunnel to Towers Foundation carries out its mission to "do good" by providing mortgage-free homes to Gold Star and fallen first responder families with young children and by building specially adapted smart homes for catastrophically injured veterans and first responders," according to the press release. "Children of the Foundation’s home recipients are offered full scholarships for undergraduate degrees and accredited trade school programs, helping secure their futures. The Foundation is also committed to eradicating veteran homelessness and helping America Never Forget September 11, 2001."

articles.title: An extraordinary result - why did MPs reject assisted dying bill this time?
articles.summary: Although supporters say they will try again, for now the momentum has fallen away from a change in the law.
articles.body:
There were gasps and – to the intense irritation of supporters – cheers from opponents of assisted dying when the vote was read out in the Commons.

The debate itself was tetchier, more irritable than when Kim Leadbeater introduced a similar bill in 2024. Then it was the first time MPs had voted on assisted dying in nine years.

Since then the Commons has voted on this issue three times and had hours of debate. The sombre, respectful tone from 2024 has become more embittered.

Given the strength of feeling on both sides over such an emotive issue, perhaps that is unsurprising.

But on a deeply divided issue, both sides agree on why the result was different.

"We always said it would come to turnout and it did," one supporter of the bill text me. An opponent messaged to say the same.

Last time MPs voted on assisted dying in June, 315 were in favour and 291 against. Today, the numbers opposed were similar: 286.

But support for this bill has ebbed away. Just 270 voted for this bill, a fall of 45.

So why have fewer MPs backed it, compared to a year ago?

There are a number of reasons why support for assisted dying has dropped off.

Some MPs have changed their mind. Janet Daby, the Labour MP for Lewisham East, for example told the Commons that after she previously backed the bill "my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill."

But in reality those switching their position are a small minority.

For others, the influence of Andy Burnham may have been a factor. When MPs last gave their collective view on assisted dying, Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister and supportive of this bill.

Burnham, however, is not. For Labour MPs wanting to follow Downing Street's priorities, abstaining might have seemed a more appealing option.

There will be other reasons why supportive MPs did not turn up today. A wedding, I'm told, took some away from Westminster. A trip to Ukraine meant others missed the vote.

Already those in favour of a change in the law promise to try again. Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original legislation last year, has told the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year.

Supporters have told me they see this parliament, with such a large proportion of Labour MPs who tend to support assisted dying, as a "unique moment" to pass this change.

"This result doesn't mean there isn't still a majority in parliament in favour of the principle of assisted dying," said one of those behind the bill.

But for now the momentum has fallen away from a change in the law.

That is a relief to those who worry such a change would risk harming vulnerable people. But it is a bitter disappointment to those who see it as a necessary and compassionate alternative to the status quo.

That bitterness from supporters is aimed in part at the House of Lords.

It was opponents' efforts there that ultimately led to this defeat. And it could hasten those calling for reform of Parliament's second chamber.

articles.summary: US News: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani arrived at the 9/11 Memorial & Museum at Ground Zero on Friday to attend the 25th anniversary commemoration of the S.
articles.body: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani arrived at the 9/11 Memorial & Museum at Ground Zero on Friday to attend the 25th anniversary commemoration of the September 11, 2001, terror attacks, despite calls from some victims' families and former New York mayor Rudy Giuliani to stay away from the ceremony.Mamdani was later seen shaking hands with Giuliani at the remembrance ceremony, with the two appearing cordial before briefly parting ways.The interaction came days after Giuliani had publicly said Mamdani's presence at the ceremony would "offend him" and urged the city's first Muslim mayor not to attend.The annual remembrance ceremony, hosted by the 9/11 Memorial & Museum, is attended by victims' families, first responders, dignitaries and other invited guests. Vice President JD Vance and former presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama, Bill Clinton and George W. Bush were also expected to attend.Calls for Mamdani to stay awayMamdani's attendance had faced opposition from some relatives of 9/11 victims. A petition launched by victims' family members urging him not to attend had gathered roughly 110,000 signatures.The campaign against his attendance largely focused on Mamdani's appointment of Ramzi Kassem as New York City's chief legal counsel. Kassem had previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, an Al Qaeda operative who pleaded guilty to war-crimes charges.Former New York governor George Pataki had also echoed calls for Mamdani to stay away from the ceremony, while Giuliani had criticised the mayor's decision to attend.The controversy intensified after Mamdani handed a ceremonial pen used to sign 9/11-related executive orders to NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch and asked her to pass it to Kassem. Critics on social media characterised the move as disrespectful to relatives of those killed in the attacks.Mamdani defends attendanceMamdani has defended his decision to attend the ceremony, saying the focus should remain on the families who lost loved ones, first responders and New Yorkers who came together after the attacks."I'm proud to be the mayor of this city. I love this city. I love this country," Mamdani said, adding that he wanted the week to focus on the families whose loved ones were killed 25 years ago, as well as first responders who gave everything to the city.The mayor had also faced criticism over his past comments and associations related to the Israel-Palestine conflict and 9/11.He has since called Twitch streamer Hasan Piker's comments that America "deserved 9/11" "objectionable and reprehensible" and said he would discourage people from using the phrase "globalize the intifada."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US warns Americans to stay vigilant as terror risk looms at major vacation hot spot
articles.summary: An updated travel advisory for Italy cites terrorism threats and petty crime such as pickpocketing on public transportation in popular tourist locations.
articles.body: Americans are being warned to exercise increased caution when traveling to one of Europe's most popular tourist destinations amid multiple terrorism-related arrests in recent months. The State Department updated its "Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution" travel advisory for Italy on Thursday — keeping the country at the same advisory level while revising its summary. Italy draws millions of visitors with its beaches, quaint villages and iconic ancient Roman landmarks. TOURIST HOT SPOT SLAPPED WITH US TRAVEL WARNING RENEWAL DUE TO CRIME AND TERROR But despite its appeal to tourists, the State Department is warning travelers to remain vigilant due to the threat of terrorism. "There is risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Italy," the advisory said. While the threat of terrorism in Italy may receive less attention than in other parts of Europe, authorities have made several terrorism-related arrests in recent months. In August, Italian news agency ANSA reported that a 16-year-old in northern Italy was arrested on international terrorism-related charges after investigators said he had spread jihadist and pro-ISIS material online. SEXUAL ASSAULTS AND SCAMS PLAGUE TOP VACATION HOT SPOT, PROMPTING URGENT ADVISORY In a separate incident in June, another 16-year-old near Bologna was arrested after authorities allegedly found jihadist material and weapons-making manuals in his possession. The State Department advisory noted that petty crime is also a significant concern in Italy, especially "in popular tourist locations and on public transportation, including trains." "Stay aware of your surroundings," officials said. Americans who decide to travel to Italy are urged to monitor local media for breaking news and "stay alert in tourist spots." articles.title: ‘Handcuffed and blindfolded’: Is the US targeting Ecuadorian fishermen?
articles.summary: A growing number of fishermen say their boats have been struck by US forces as Trump expands his anti-drug campaign.
articles.body:
Manta, Ecuador – Jose Hernan Flores is still trying to recover from what he describes as a hostile encounter with United States forces at sea.

Flores is a fisherman from the town of San Mateo, along Ecuador’s Pacific coast.

In March, he was out on the water with his crew of 16, piloting his vessel, La Negra Francisca Duarte II, to chase schools of fish.

Suddenly, a group of military-style drones appeared in the sky. They swooped towards La Negra Francisca Duarte II.

“We saw drones exploding on the ship, and we did not understand what was going on. Two of our sailors were injured,” Flores told Al Jazeera.

As La Negra Francisca Duarte II caught fire, Flores and his crew abandoned ship, escaping onto smaller boats, known as skiffs, used to help with their fishing.

“We jumped on the smaller vessels to try to get assistance,” Flores explained.

But as they approached what appeared to be a nearby tuna vessel, Flores realised its occupants were not fishermen at all. They were soldiers.

“They had beards and had US military uniforms. They handcuffed and blindfolded us. They had drones and all sorts of military equipment,” Flores said.

The soldiers helped treat those injured in Flores’s crew and then handed them over to a navy unit from El Salvador. The fishermen were at sea for at least another week until they were brought ashore. Later, they were deported back to Ecuador.

Flores says his boat, valued at around $400,000, was completely destroyed. He is still paying off the loan he took out to buy it.

His story is one of dozens from Ecuadorian fishermen who claim they too were attacked by the US at sea.

While the US military has denied responsibility for the sinking of Flores’s boat, the North American country has adopted an increasingly aggressive approach to what it considers to be maritime drug-trafficking.

Since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term, the Pentagon has carried out dozens of strikes on small vessels in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, many of them lethal.

The Trump administration has argued that such attacks are necessary to combat “narco-terrorism”. But fishermen say they are coming under fire for no discernable reason.

Positioned between the two largest coca-growing regions in the world — Colombia and Peru — Ecuador has become one of the most important transit points for cocaine leaving South America.

It has therefore emerged as a crucial ally in Trump’s campaign against drug-trafficking organisations.

This week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio toured Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, in part to generate support for the US fight against criminal groups in the region.

In Quito, Rubio said the Trump administration would seek $45m in additional security funding for Ecuador and deliver more military equipment to President Daniel Noboa’s right-wing government.

He also confirmed that “elite forces” from the US were working with Ecuador to dismantle what he called “terrorist organisations”.

“I think it’s important to point out, for a second, that the groups we are taking on, these are terrorist organisations. These are not just criminal organisations,” Rubio said.

But many in Ecuador are concerned about their country’s coopereation with the US military is affecting communities in the region.

Earlier this month, in the fishing village of Santa Marianita, dozens of people gathered on the coast to demand justice for the fishermen who have been attacked.

Lourdes Mero’s husband and son have been missing for months. The Fiorella, the fishing vessel they were travelling on, disappeared near the Galapagos Islands in January.

Eight of the boat’s 10 crew have been missing ever since. The two survivors had been piloting skiffs to lay bait when they said they lost contact with the Fiorella. They reportedly saw smoke rising on the horizon.

The missing men’s families still do not know whether their loved ones are dead or alive.

“My husband has heart disease, and I don’t know what to do. Please return my family to me,” Mero said during an interview with Al Jazeera.

“We need the eight crew members back. We don’t know where they are. We are asking the government, but nobody tells us anything.”

According to The Washington Post, the operation was part of a covert US programme led by the Cental Intelligence Agency (CIA), targeting vessels suspected of drug trafficking.

But the US has never publicly acknowledged carrying out any attack against the Fiorella.

Fishing communities on the Pacific coast say they are how caught between two threats: US operations at sea and criminal organisations that use ports for drug trafficking.

Cesar Delgado is from the Manta Crew Members Association, a professional group based in Manta, one of Ecuador’s largest hubs for tuna fishing.

He explained that many fishermen are now afraid to go out to sea, in case they are mistaken for drug traffickers and targeted by US forces.

“Eighty percent of the fleet is not at sea but right on the port. Our fishermen are running out of work. People are losing their ships,” Delgado said.

He called on the US government to provide evidence for its allegations that it targeting drug-trafficking vessels, not fishermen.

“If they have proof that there are drugs, they should show it — not sink the boat, which is what they are doing,” Delgado added.

The US has acknowledged intercepting some boats. As recently as Tuesday, US Southern Command, which oversees military operations in Latin America, announced it had intercepted a “floating refueling station” it claims was linked to Los Choneros, an Ecuadorian gang.

After removing the individuals on board, the US military said it proceeded to sink the boat.

In such cases, the US has indicated it transfers suspects back to Ecuadorian authorities. But those detentions may have fallen short of legal standards.

On Saturday, a judge in Ecuador ordered the release of 28 fishermen, ruling there was not enough evidence to keep them in custody. Other cases are currently being investigated.

But critics say the harm goes beyond Ecuador’s fishing communities. As the US expands its security footprint, concerns are likewise growing about the future of Latin American sovereignty under Trump — and Washington’s adherence to the rule of law.

articles.title: Gen Zs recall first learning of 'deeply harrowing, terrifying' 9/11
articles.summary: They carry distinct memories not from the day itself, but from the moment  - years later - they learned about the attacks.
articles.body:
Most Americans remember exactly what they were doing and how they felt the day four airplanes were hijacked and crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and a field in Pennsylvania.

But now, 25 years on from the 11 September 2001 attacks , there is a new generation, too young to remember the day that permanently altered much of American life.

Members of Generation Z, born between 1997 and 2012, were told - well after the fact - about the event that undoubtedly reshaped their futures.

They carry distinct memories not from the day itself, but from the moment years later that they learned about the attacks.

'Hard to explain what a terrorist is to a child'

Avery Black, 20, a journalism student at the University of South Carolina, remembers hearing about 9/11 for the first time in elementary school, then going home and asking her mother about it, she told the BBC.

"She just started telling me where she was the day it happened, and just broke down in tears, explaining to me about all the firefighters that went in and never came out," Black recalled.

As a child, Black didn't quite grasp the day's gravity, but for her, certain details still stand out.

She remembers, most distinctly, the "falling man" – a famous image of a man plummeting, upside down, from the North Tower. A Dallas, Texas native, she also recalls teachers showing the video of then-President George W. Bush first learning about the attacks at an elementary school event.

For Annie Erickson, 26, who grew up in North Carolina, personal anecdotes, more than school or reports, created her first memories of 9/11.

"My mother grew up in New York City, so I remember my mom telling me about 9/11 and talking about how someone that lived in her building, who she was friends with, passed away in the towers," Erickson said.

She also was struck when learning about 9/11 at school that it was one of the few historical events teachers could personalise with their own memories.

Currently, there's no national requirement for US schools to teach students about the attacks, and the expectations vary widely by state. Twenty-five states require or expect public schools to teach the events of 9/11, while 13 make 9/11 instruction optional, according to a recent analysis by The Associated Press.

But not every state that requires it specifies a curriculum.

Allegra Tashjian, who grew up in Wisconsin, said her teacher explained in first or second grade that it was a very important, sombre day and asked if anyone knew why. After a student responded that it was the day planes hit the towers in New York, Tashjian wondered why she had never heard of it before.

Later, at home, she recalls finding her mom folding laundry and asking if she remembered planes crashing in New York. "I remember she kind of paused folding her laundry and was like, 'um no, I don't think I've ever heard anything about that,'" the now-28-year-old PhD student said.

"For whatever reason at that point, I guess she really didn't want to talk about it."

Tashjian, Erickson, Black and several other Gen Zs all told the BBC that they remember hearing a few details about the attacks in school and from their families, but only through their own research did they learn in depth what actually happened that day.

"I really understood the gravity of it more from reading things on the internet when I was probably between like nine and 12", Tashjian said.

Black didn't realise at first who was behind the attack. "That was the part that I wasn't really taught until I did my own research. It's really hard to explain what a terrorist is to a child."

Professor David Schanzer, who teaches "9/11 & Its Aftermath" at Duke University, wrote this week in a campus magazine commentary that there's still strong interest generations later. His course is full, with dozens on a waitlist.

"Ten years ago, I thought student interest was ebbing and I would need to find something else to teach about," he said.

But current world events, he said, only made young people more curious about what happened 25 years ago on 9/11.

"If you want to understand what has gone wrong over the past couple of decades it makes sense to learn about 9/11, the first global catastrophe of the 21st century (the others being the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic)," he wrote.

Different generation, different approach

Several Gen Zs told the BBC that, despite gaining knowledge about the tragicday, it is still common among peers to actively lighten conversations about 9/11.

Thomas Schwartz, a professor of history and political science at Vanderbilt University, said in a recent class discussion, his seniors - born in 2004 or 2005 - remarked on their generation's tendency to "deflect and joke about 9/11".

He added that "students from the Northeast, who had parents with personal memories of 9/11, were more careful about this, remarking on the sensitivities in their family about the subject."

Erickson said many Gen Zs tend to downplay monumental events or tragedies because either they "can't fully understand their impact" or they're using humour as a coping mechanism "to not have to think too deeply about some of the larger anxieties in our world".

Even now as an adult, Tashjian said it's still difficult for her to fathom large numbers of people dying in any event, and she still gravitates toward individual anecdotes to help her understand 9/11's toll.

Schanzer contends that learning about 9/11 and understanding its impact remains crucial for younger generations without first-hand knowledge.

"But like most significant historical events, one can't fully understand our world today unless you understand why 9/11 occurred and how the United States responded to it," he said.

articles.title: A 27-year-old Tennessee diesel mechanic wanted to farm full-time; solar sites gave his sheep 400+ acres to graze, letting him quit his job and build a 300-ewe flock
articles.summary: US News: A 27-year-old Tennessee diesel mechanic has left his job to become a full-time livestock farmer after gaining grazing access to more than 400 acres of.
articles.body: A 27-year-old Tennessee diesel mechanic has left his job to become a full-time livestock farmer after gaining grazing access to more than 400 acres of utility-scale solar farms. The arrangement, made through vegetation management contracts at solar sites, allowed the young farmer to expand his flock to more than 300 breeding ewes without having to buy the large amount of land usually needed for a commercial sheep operation. According to regional advocacy group Appalachian Voices, solar grazing, also known as agrivoltaics, is creating new opportunities for small livestock farmers across the American South. The practice involves using sheep to control grass and weeds growing beneath and around ground-mounted solar panels. Solar companies avoid using fuel-powered mowing equipment, while farmers gain access to fenced pasture through long-term grazing agreements.High land prices make farming difficult for young producersFinding enough affordable pasture remains one of the biggest challenges for people trying to start commercial livestock farms in the United States. In East and Middle Tennessee, rising land prices and suburban growth have pushed the cost of farmland beyond the reach of many young farmers. Those without inherited family property or large amounts of capital can struggle to purchase enough acreage to make livestock farming financially viable. High equipment costs and expensive land rentals can also force young farmers to keep full-time jobs outside agriculture. That often leaves farming as a smaller side business rather than a full-time career. Solar farms can provide another option through vegetation management agreements. Developers usually surround their facilities with strong fencing and may install water systems. They also plant grass and clover between rows of solar panels, creating pasture that can be used by grazing animals. Sheep can then be brought onto the site to keep vegetation under control. Keeping grass below the lower edge of the solar panels helps prevent plants from interfering with the panels while avoiding the need for heavy mowing equipment. Using sheep also reduces the risk of machinery damaging solar equipment. Tractors and mowers can potentially strike panels, support structures or other equipment, while sheep can graze around the installations without causing the same risks.Solar grazing creates benefits for both sidesSheep grazing on solar farms is becoming a growing partnership between renewable energy companies and local farmers. Research and reporting by Appalachian Voices found that solar operators can reduce vegetation maintenance costs by using local shepherds to manage grass and weeds. Farmers, meanwhile, receive access to pasture and an additional source of income. Sheep are particularly suited to solar facilities because of their size. Unlike cattle and horses, sheep can move under relatively low solar panel structures and graze around steel support posts. Their smaller size also allows them to reach areas where standard mowing equipment may have difficulty operating safely. For the Tennessee producer, income from vegetation management contracts provided the financial security needed to leave his diesel mechanic job and work full-time with his livestock. Access to more than 400 acres of solar pasture gave him enough space to grow his breeding flock to more than 300 ewes. The large area also made rotational grazing possible. Under this system, sheep are moved between different fenced sections of pasture, giving grass time to recover. Rotational grazing can also help reduce parasite pressure by preventing animals from repeatedly grazing the same areas.Solar grazing expands across the USThe growth of sheep grazing on solar farms in Tennessee is part of a wider trend across the US renewable energy industry. Data from the American Solar Grazing Association shows that livestock are now being used to manage vegetation across tens of thousands of acres of solar installations in the country. Sheep grazing is being used at utility-scale solar facilities in more than two dozen states. The practice is creating additional contract income for livestock farmers while providing solar companies with an alternative to conventional vegetation management. Agrivoltaic sites can also provide environmental benefits. Reported benefits include higher organic matter in topsoil, better water retention and lower emissions from mowing equipment. Pastures managed around solar installations can also support soil organisms and pollinators when flowering plants are allowed to grow between grazing cycles. Advocates at Appalachian Voices say combining agriculture with solar development can also reduce some of the land-use concerns surrounding large renewable energy projects.Instead of removing farmland entirely from agricultural use, solar sites can continue supporting livestock production while generating electricity. This approach can be particularly important in rural communities where residents are concerned that large solar developments could replace traditional family farms. With more solar projects expected across the Tennessee Valley and the wider Appalachian region in the coming years, agricultural organisations expect solar grazing to become a larger part of the region's farming economy. For young farmers facing high land prices, the model offers something that can be difficult to find: access to large areas of pasture without having to buy them outright.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Texas man remembered by Fox News hosts after repeat offender arrested in savage park bench slaying
articles.summary: Surveillance video captured the fatal Round Rock, Texas, stabbing of Andrew James Wimsatt on a park bench moments after visiting his mother nearby.
articles.body: A 62-year-old Texas engineer with ties to multiple Fox News hosts was stabbed to death from behind in what authorities have described as a random attack on a park bench in Round Rock, Texas, and deputies have arrested a repeat offender who spent months in the local jail earlier this year. Andrew James Wimsatt, of Austin, was killed on Sept. 7 — minutes after he sat down in the park after visiting his mother at a nursing home nearby, according to authorities. Williamson County deputies have arrested a 26-year-old local man named Benedict Chinedu Ogbodiegwu on murder and theft charges. GOT A TIP? The murder was recorded on surveillance video, according to the Williamson County Sheriff's Office. A man identified as Wimsatt sat down on a park bench at around 11 a.m., authorities said. A few minutes later, another man, alleged to be Ogbodiegwu, grabbed him from behind and repeatedly drove a knife into his neck. The victim struggled but was unable to push his attacker away as the stabbing continued, according to a probable cause affidavit obtained by Fox 7 Austin. The suspect then wiped the blood off on his shirt and walked out of view. REPEAT OFFENDER BUSTED AGAIN LESS THAN 24 HOURS AFTER RELEASE IN BRAZEN JEWELRY STORE THEFT CASE: POLICE Wimsatt, who had a Ph.D. in civil engineering, is credited on IMDB as an executive producer of the Penn Jillette horror/comedy "Director's Cut." He worked for the Texas A&M Transportation Institute, staying on part-time even after retiring, and had an Instagram account filled with photos of wildlife, vintage storefronts and city landscapes. He also had ties to several Fox News personalities. "The crime, to me, is so heinous and shocking that I’m still trying to comprehend it," Greg Gutfeld said Friday. "I may never." They first met when Wimsatt became a fan of a former show, "Red Eye," Gutfeld said. The engineer would clip segments from the show and attend his live events. "At first, I was suspicious, because I always assume people do things because they want things," he told Fox News Digital. "I was wrong with Andrew. He did stuff for people — lots of people — because he enjoyed being of service, and promoting stuff that he genuinely enjoys and believes in." Kat Timpf called him a "fan who became a friend" — a friend not only to her, but also to her family. They had lunch in Fort Worth in June, and she said she was expecting to see him at a show in Nevada later this month. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST "He was so kind and generous it almost seems impossible," she told Fox News Digital Friday. "He always supported me... whether that was sending me clips I wanted to post or offering truly helpful words of encouragement during the times throughout my career that the internet was piling on me." They spoke regularly — once a week or more for years — and he became known for sending TV clips to members of the "Gutfeld!" cast. "Whenever the rest of the internet was making me feel hopeless about the state of the world, I could always count on a message from Andrew to remind me of the good that's out there, too," Timpf said. Wimsatt attended Tyrus' standup shows as well. "[He] took care of his mother… always positive… he was kind man, 62 years old fragile looking but had a monster laugh," Tyrus said in a statement. "I was honored to know him I was honored he cared so much and honored that my jokes and thoughts brought him joy." GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL On Labor Day, a witness called 911 after finding Wimsatt on the ground in the park, and paramedics pronounced him dead at the scene, according to authorities. Investigators were able to retrace the suspect's steps and allegedly recovered prints and other evidence, including bloody clothes and the suspected murder weapon, according to the affidavit. When confronted with video evidence, Ogbodiegwu allegedly claimed he had a twin brother but could not provide his name. Ogbodiegwu has a criminal record in Williamson County going back to at least 2017, when he was charged with stealing. He had two prior arrests this year, on charges involving theft and carrying fake identification. Prior to his arrest in connection with Wimsatt's murder, he was most recently released from the county jail on June 9. He had also been incarcerated between January and April. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He's being held on $1 million bond. His next court date is on Oct. 8 at 1:30 p.m., for a pre-indictment docket call. "He was a kind, generous man, nearly beheaded in a park on a sunny morning, for no reason, just because," Gutfeld said. "I believe everyone who allowed the person who killed him to roam free like that, deserve severe accountability."

articles.title: UK lawmakers vote against bill to legalise assisted dying
articles.summary: Parliament’s lower ⁠chamber, the House of Commons, rejected the legislation by 286 votes to 270.
articles.body:
Lawmakers in the United Kingdom have voted against allowing terminally ill adults in England and Wales to choose to end their lives, dealing a setback to campaigners and bringing the latest ⁠effort to change the law to an end.

The bill known as “The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life)” was voted down on Friday with a total of 286 members of Parliament opposing the proposal and 270 voting for it.

It had proposed allowing adults with under six months to live to apply for an assisted death with the approval of at least two doctors and an expert panel.

Many individual lawmakers relayed their own stories both in favour of and against the proposal.

The government took a neutral stance, meaning lawmakers voted according to their consciences rather than along party lines.

The new UK leader, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, did not vote because he said he did not want to “unduly influence the debate”. His predecessor, Keir Starmer, who has left Parliament, was in favour of the proposed legislation.

The vote brings an end to a two-year debate in parliament about assisted dying, during which the House of Commons had backed assisted dying on two previous occasions. Their backing was not enough for it to become law because it was effectively filibustered by unelected lawmakers in the House of Lords.

Lauren Edwards, a lawmaker in Burnham’s Labour Party, had brought the legislation back through a mechanism known as a Private Member’s Bill, whereby an individual lawmaker selected in a ballot ‌can try to pass a law independently of the government.

“This is a hugely disappointing result – not for me but for the many thousands of terminally ill people and their loved ones who were given hope when the Commons voted for this Bill last year,” she said in a statement, referring to the lower house’s previous backing for the legislation.

Dignity in Dying, one of the groups campaigning for the bill, also decried Friday’s outcome as “a devastating setback for dying people”, but added: “This issue is not going away. Law change on assisted dying remains a matter of when – not if.”

Since Friday’s measure failed at its first parliamentary hurdle, it cannot be revived during the current legislative session, which is expected to run until the early next year.

Questions about safeguards for vulnerable people remain a core part of the debate, with opponents arguing the bill could expose some terminally ill people to pressure to end their lives.

Gordon Macdonald, chief executive of campaign group Care Not Killing, welcomed the result, saying lawmakers had recognised concerns that changing the law could put pressure on people to end their lives prematurely.

“Our current laws protect vulnerable people and [members of Parliament] have rightly said they do not need changing; it’s time to ⁠move beyond this debate and fix palliative care,” Macdonald added.

Parliament also rejected a similar attempt to legalise assisted dying in 2015.

A poll published by Ipsos on Monday showed two in three Britons supported the legalisation of assisted dying in principle, though in some cases that backing hinged on additional funding being provided for palliative care.

articles.title: Mayors fear tourism tax would put visitors off
articles.summary: A charge appears unlikely to be introduced in Greater Lincolnshire or in Hull and East Yorkshire.
articles.body:
Elected mayors in East Yorkshire and Lincolnshire say they have no plans to introduce a tourist tax.

Under new government plans, regional mayors in England would have the power to introduce a charge on overnight accommodation stays.

It would be an uncapped fee as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation, and the money could go towards improving high streets and local transport, the government said.

But Luke Campbell, mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire, said his "instinct" was not to implement it, while Greater Lincolnshire's Dame Andrea Jenkyns said she did not want to drive visitors away.

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , Reform UK's Campbell said he was not keen on the tax, although he added he "would never rule out an idea forever".

"I support mayors having the power because every region is different and we know our own areas best, but having the power doesn't mean you have to use it," he said.

"I've spoken directly to people running tourism and hospitality businesses here and I understand why they're worried.

"They're already dealing with enough pressure, so my instinct is not to add another cost for visitors or businesses."

Fellow Reform mayor Dame Andrea said the tax could put people off visiting the area.

"I can see how our hospitality industry has been, quite frankly, hammered over the years - the B&Bs, the hotels, the pubs and restaurants," she said.

"I do not want to drive out people from visiting our region, so I will not be implementing it."

The planned legislation will go before Parliament soon.

articles.title: Running costs of Covid vaccine damage scheme double the amount paid to victims
articles.summary: The cost of administration and medical checks has now topped £83m, according to new figures.
articles.body:
The government scheme to support people injured by Covid vaccines and other jabs has cost £83m to run since April 2022, new figures have revealed.

The amount spent on administration costs and medical assessments is more than double the £32m paid out in financial support to victims so far.

The Taxpayers' Alliance think tank said the public would be "stunned" at the cost and called for the government to urgently review the scheme.

NHSBSA which runs the scheme for the government says rising numbers of claims are behind the increasing administrative and medical assessor supplier costs.

Firm assessing Covid vaccine harm replaced after costs spiral to £48m

Families failed by Covid jabs tell inquiry of pain

The latest data shows there have been 24,260 claims since November 2021, although just 264 have been successful.

The Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS) was set up in 1979 to provide financial support to people who, in rare cases, had been harmed by vaccines of any type.

Since the pandemic the number applying for damage payments has increased sharply.

The vast majority of applications are now linked to the AstraZeneca vaccine and other Covid jabs.

The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But for those who were harmed, the resulting injuries are devastating.

The full costs of the VDPS have now been revealed for the first time in the answer to a parliamentary question from the backbench Conservative MP Sir Christopher Chope.

In response, health minister Dame Diana Johnson said a total of £83m had been spent on staffing costs, administration and medical reviews between April 2022 and March 2026.

Under the scheme, claimants must have their application reviewed by an independent doctor, to check whether they have met the threshold of "severe disablement".

If approved, they can then receive a one-off, tax-free payment of £120,000. The process can take months or even years.

The costs of those medical assessments have increased from £4.3m in 2022/23 to £19.3m in 2025/26, according to new data published by the government.

Based on the latest available data up to June 2026, the total amount paid out in damages to those who died or were injured after being given a Covid vaccine has risen to £31.6m.

"The administrative costs and medical assessor supplier costs of the VDPS are driven by the number of claims received," said the NHSBSA, which runs the scheme on behalf of the government.

"We have seen a significant increase in the number of claims received since taking over administration of the VDPS in November 2021."

The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose.

"It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.

Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme.

Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered.

The government is due to respond to her recommendations.

The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments.

The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed".

"When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell.

He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help."

The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly".

"In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said.

NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS".
