articles.title: US holds memorials for the 9/11 attacks, 25 years later
articles.summary: In New York, Virginia and Pennsylvania, mourners gathered to remember nearly 3,000 people killed during the hijackings.
articles.body:
To mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks, Americans gathered to remember the nearly 3,000 people killed when hijacked planes struck the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania.

The most prominent event on Friday was arguably at Ground Zero, the site in New York City where the landmark World Trade Center, known as the Twin Towers, once stood.

The buildings collapsed after two commercial jets crashed into them as part of the hijacking. A memorial and museum now sit at the site. During Friday’s ceremony, relatives of victims read the names of those killed as they have every year since the attack, surrounded by the two reflecting pools that mark the towers’ footprints.

In Arlington, Virginia, mourners also gathered at the Pentagon, where American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the building, killing 184. United States President Donald Trump and Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth were among those delivering remarks.

“In those harrowing days after the attacks, we saw the authentic spirit of our nation. We were all New Yorkers that day, every one of us,” Trump said at the Pentagon ceremony. “The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail and to win.”

Families also came together in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, for an observance in honour of the passengers and crew killed aboard United Airlines Flight 93.

While it is believed the attackers aimed to crash the plane in Washington, DC, they faced a revolt from those trapped on the aircraft with them. The plane ultimately made a nosedive into a rural field, instead of hitting the attackers’ target. Forty victims were killed.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro ordered flags in the state to fly at half-staff, to “honor the bravery of the men and women who stood up to evil and ran towards danger while others were running away”.

The attacks on September 11 marked a new era for the United States, ushering in the “global war on terror”, a decades-long effort that involved US-led wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

There have also been lifelong consequences for survivors of the attack. Earlier this week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani released government documents indicating that city officials knew about the risks of toxic exposure after the fall of the Twin Towers.

An estimated 400,000 people were exposed to chemicals including carcinogens, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Thousands are believed to have died from conditions like cancer in the quarter century since the attacks.

articles.summary: South Asia News: Dehradun: More than 800 litres of free petrol and diesel have reached hospitals, relief camps and people in flood-hit parts of Nepal through a three-m.
articles.body: Dehradun: More than 800 litres of free petrol and diesel have reached hospitals, relief camps and people in flood-hit parts of Nepal through a three-member volunteer team from the US, which even used heavy-lift drones and zip-lines to move fuel into areas where roads and access routes had been washed away. The volunteers, working with the Fuel Relief Fund (FRF), have spent the past five days procuring fuel locally and distributing it according to need, while also supplying LPG cylinders to relief camps running community kitchens.Joseph Lee, a retired firefighter from Texas, and two other FRF volunteers travelled to Nepal as part of the organisation’s disaster-response effort. Lee told TOI that FRF, a volunteer-based organisation operating since 2005, had supplied fuel during nearly 30 disasters, including earthquakes in Turkey, Venezuela, Nepal and Haiti, besides emergencies in Morocco, Mozambique, the Philippines and the US. “Our organisation works purely on funds raised through donations,” he said.Lee said FRF used those donations to buy fuel from local sources in disaster-hit countries rather than transporting supplies from abroad. “We have so far distributed more than 800 litres of petrol and diesel to people and agencies in need. We understand the value of this critical resource in situations like this, and our priorities are hospitals and relief camps,” he said.Connectivity remained the biggest challenge, with several roads and approaches destroyed by the floods. “We have transported free fuel using heavy-lift drones and zip-lines where accessibility was washed away, and we also work with local associates to make sure it reaches those who actually need it,” Lee said.His co-volunteer Katherine said the team had also supplied LPG cylinders to remote relief camps after community kitchens began running short of cooking fuel. “Many community kitchens were short of cooking fuel, so we provided LPG cylinders to ensure survivors continued getting meals. We will continue despite the challenges,” she said.Lee said five more FRF volunteers would join the team in Nepal within days, expanding its relief operations. On Thursday, the group left with 210 litres of fuel for Dhunche, one of the areas badly affected by the floods, despite difficult road conditions. “Reaching there is difficult because of the poor roads, but we are determined to extend our help,” he said.Saurab Rimal, founder of Nepal-based NGO Karmayog Foundation, which is also involved in relief work, praised the initiative. “What they are doing is really appreciable in this situation. I haven’t seen anyone else doing this so far,” he said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
articles.summary: In New York, the Pentagon and Pennsylvania, solemn ceremonies commemorate the landmark anniversary.
articles.body:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, US presidents past and present have commemorated the lives lost when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while US Vice-President JD Vance attended a memorial at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, along with all four living former US presidents and first ladies.

Moments of silence were held to mark the timings of the attacks and the names of nearly 3,000 people who died were read out.

Commemorations were also held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where Flight 93 crashed after passengers fought back against the hijackers.

George W Bush, who was president at the time of the attacks, was joined by former Presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton at Friday's ceremony.

At the Pentagon, President Trump attended a commemoration alongside cabinet secretaries and Condoleezza Rice, who was US secretary of state on 9/11.

"Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago," Trump said. "We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today."

He sought to link the "war on terror" that followed 9/11, which sparked years of US involvement in Middle East wars, with his current conflict in Iran.

Trump told the crowd that the Islamic Republic "will never, ever have a nuclear weapon".

Gen Zs recall first learning of 'deeply harrowing, terrifying' 9/11

9/11: What happened and how many people died in September 11 attacks?

Janice Brooks had only moved to New York a couple of weeks before 9/11 to begin what she calls "the biggest adventure", working for a company on the 84th floor of the South Tower of the World Trade Center.

She told the BBC she was in the office when the first plane hit the North Tower. While she was evacuating, the second plane hit with an "almighty thud".

Brooks said she heard "one of those horror film screams" as a woman was hit by debris. She looked up and saw a "big gaping hole" where her office should have been.

Every year on 11 September, bells ring to commemorate the exact time that each of the four planes crashed, and the exact time the Twin Towers fell.

Each of the six bells is followed by a moment of silence.

This year, a seventh bell was rung to commemorate the thousands who died from diseases including cancer after the attacks.

Illnesses related to dust and smoke from the towers' collapse have since claimed more than threefold the nearly 3,000 lives lost in the attacks, US health officials say.

As the names of the dead were read out for nearly four hours at the ceremony in Manhattan, a 9/11 widow criticised Saudi Arabia and what she characterised as failures by US officials to hold the kingdom accountable.

"You are missed more with each year that passes," Terry Strada said of her husband Tom Strada in remarks broadcast live worldwide.

"But how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?"

The comments by Mrs Strada, national chairperson of 9/11 Families United, drew applause from the audience.

The majority of those who carried out the 9/11 attacks were from Saudi Arabia and planning was led by al-Qaeda founder Osama Bin-Laden, scion of a prominent Saudi family.

But Saudi officials have repeatedly denied any involvement in the attacks, and in 2004 the 9/11 Commission Report cleared the country of any involvement.

Events were also held elsewhere to honour the victims. In London, there was a ceremonial event at Buckingham Palace attended by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the US ambassador Warren Stephens.

The Toronto Stock Exchange also held an event to remember colleagues who died in the attacks.

In Gander, Newfoundland, the US ambassador to Canada praised the small town that took in thousands of passengers from 38 diverted planes in the hours after the attack.

"When people in America hear the word Gander, our hearts soften," Pete Hoekstra said.

"As a representative of the United States government, thank you for your friendship... to the nation of Canada, thank you for being a partner and for the shared sacrifices that you made with us."

His remarks come amid fraught relations between the US and Canada, with the two countries engaged in a trade war. Ahead of the 9/11 commemorations, some Gander residents had called for Hoekstra's invite to be rescinded.

Still, Hoekstra's speech was met with applause. But in separate remarks afterwards, former Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chrétien said: "I have message for American friends... never mistake our generosity for weakness." He received a standing ovation.

In Milan, a group of Italian and US firefighters participated in a ceremonial stair climb to honour the emergency responders who died in the line of duty.

Dressed in their uniforms and carrying equipment, they climbed 110 floors up and down the Galfa Tower, in remembrance of the number of storeys on each of the Twin Towers.

articles.title: At least 46,000 displaced by escalating Yemen fighting: UN
articles.summary: The International Organisation for Migration (IOM) warns that the figure is rising ‘by the hour’.
articles.body:
More than 46,000 people have been driven from their homes in Yemen in the wake of the latest escalation in fighting between Houthi rebels and government forces, according to United Nations data.

The International Organisation for Migration (IOM) warned that the figure is rising “by the hour” in a statement issued on Friday.

The UN agency called on all parties to the conflict to guarantee safe humanitarian access and protect civilians, aid workers and humanitarian assets on the ground.

“Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left,” Amy Pope, head of the IOM, said in the statement.

The agency said many people had reportedly fled Mocha with their belongings overnight after the Iran-allied Houthi rebels captured the strategically important Red Sea port city from the internationally recognised government on Thursday .

Entire villages were said to have been abandoned in some areas of the war-torn country. The IOM urged the parties to the conflict to guarantee humanitarian access and ensure the safety of aid workers.

The statement came amid reports on Friday that the Houthis had captured a strategically located island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and now control Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast.

Separately on Friday, the UN also voiced concern over the Houthis seizing a key humanitarian compound and its assets in Mocha, warning that humanitarian personnel and facilities must be protected.

“The compound houses staff of UN agencies working to provide humanitarian assistance to vulnerable communities in the area,” UN deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq told reporters.

All UN personnel working at the compound had left before the seizure and were “safe and accounted for”, Haq added.

Haq stressed that humanitarian personnel, premises and assets “must be respected and protected at all times”, while calling for safe and unimpeded humanitarian access so life-saving assistance can continue reaching people in need.

Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen researcher at the London-based Chatham House thinktank, told Al Jazeera that deteriorating humanitarian conditions in Yemen will build on what was already one of the world’s worst crises.

“Yemen was already going through one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world,” Al-Muslimi said.

“It got terribly worse after the Houthis cracked down on aid organisations in northern Yemen. But the war continued despite the fragile truce, and what that meant was the destruction of what remained of the economy, with millions of families left without income,” he said.

Al-Muslimi warned that the latest escalation “will create two new crises”, one being further internal displacement, noting that “we’ve already seen more than 10,000 families displaced in the last week alone”, and the other being rising prices for goods inside Yemen.

“Since this is [happening in] a maritime [trade] corridor, it will, for sure, drive further violence inside Yemen, but also from outside Yemen,” Al-Muslimi added.

“The Yemeni population will continue to suffer, first and foremost, more than anyone else, inside or outside the country.”

articles.title: Kansas renews Border War rivalry with Missouri by calling Tigers 'evil,' invoking slavery imagery
articles.summary: Kansas dropped a hype video calling Missouri evil over Civil War history ahead of Friday's Border Showdown, and critics say it went too far.
articles.body: You all know I'm a sucker for college football rivalries. I even wrote about some of my favorite rivalries in the sport that are no longer annual contests, and one of the games that ended up on that list was Kansas vs. Missouri, so you can imagine my excitement when it was announced that these two foes would be going at it once more. The Border War, as it was known until 2004, dates back to 1891 and features the kind of hatred and bad blood that makes college football rivalries hit differently than any other sport. NOTRE DAME-USC RIVALRY GAME DISCUSSIONS BACK ON AFTER COLLEGE FOOTBALL SERIES ENDED IN 2026 That hatred was on full display thanks to a new hype video the Jayhawks dropped on social media earlier this week in anticipation for Friday's showdown, and, if we are being honest, they might have taken things just a bit too far. Listen, I'm all for animus in college football rivalries but calling Mizzou evil because Missouri was a slave state 160 years ago feels a bit much, don't you think? I love how they had to officially change the name from Border War to Border Showdown so as not to invoke images of armed conflict, but here comes the Kansas social media team saying, "Hey, remember the Civil War? Well, our opponent was on the side that wanted to keep using slaves." That's painting with a bit of a broad brush, if you ask me. Also, no one at the University of Missouri, be they students, faculty, or otherwise, were even alive at the time of the Civil War, so I'm not sure it's very polite or even correct to call them all "evil." Most of the Mizzou players featured in Kansas's hype video are black, too, and I can assure you they didn't commit to the Tigers because they're pro slavery. And the final cherry on top of this embarrassment sundae is that Metro Boomin, the producer for the song "Superhero (Heroes & Villains)" used in the video, is from, you guessed it, Missouri. articles.title: 'Will work with India, be friends': China ahead of PM Modi-Xi meeting in Delhi
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival in New Delhi for the ongoing Brics Summit, Chinese Ambassador to India Xu Feihong said on F.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival in New Delhi for the ongoing Brics Summit, Chinese Ambassador to India Xu Feihong said on Friday that China will work with India to ensure the two countries remain “friends enjoying good-neighbourliness and partners helping each other succeed.”"China and India are arranging a bilateral meeting between President Xi and Prime Minister Modi. This will be the third consecutive year that the two leaders have met, following their meetings in Kazan and Tianjin,” the Chinese ambassador wrote on X.“China will work with India to implement the strategic guidance of the two leaders, approach bilateral relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, strengthen communication, enhance cooperation, properly manage differences, and remain friends enjoying good-neighborliness and partners helping each other succeed,” he added.Xi will arrive in New Delhi on Saturday to attend the Brics Summit, marking his first visit to India in nearly seven years. He is scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting with PM Modi on the sidelines of the summit.The Chinese leader’s visit is expected to be a high-profile diplomatic engagement, with implications for ongoing efforts to stabilise bilateral ties between New Delhi and Beijing following the military clashes in Ladakh in 2020.Xi last visited India in 2019 for an informal summit with PM Modi in Mamallapuram near Chennai.He had earlier visited Goa in 2016 to attend the Brics Summit and made his first visit to India in September 2014, when he held extensive talks with PM Modi. The 2014 visit took place during the first terms of both leaders.Xi’s forthcoming visit is significant as it comes amid efforts by India and China to normalise relations after a prolonged freeze following the 2020 standoff. PM Modi met Xi in Kazan, Russia, in 2024 during that year’s Brics Summit. The two leaders met again in September last year during PM Modi’s visit to China for an SCO Summit in Tianjin.As the current chair of the grouping, India will host the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi on September 12 and 13.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2021, China built its first plastic road using 6,000 milk bottles; the result turned hard-to-recycle plastic waste into useful paving material
articles.summary: China News: In 2021, thousands of used milk bottles in Shanghai found a second life. More than 6,000 bottles, along with other plastic waste, were used in a road .
articles.body: In 2021, thousands of used milk bottles in Shanghai found a second life. More than 6,000 bottles, along with other plastic waste, were used in a road project at East China University of Science and Technology, turning material that recyclers often struggled to accept into part of a polymer-modified asphalt surface. The project, unveiled on Earth Day, was developed by Dow and dairy brand Shiny Meadow to tackle the problem of hard-to-recycle plastic. Instead of ending up as waste, the bottles were processed for road paving, offering an unusual route for plastic that had little value in conventional recycling.Why milk bottles were hard to recycleAccording to the official Dow press release, milk bottles might be suitable for recycling. The bottles were technically recyclable, but recyclers are often unwilling to accept them because leftover milk residue caused a high rate of contamination. That meant a material that could be recycled could still end up being treated as waste rather than as a useful resource.Shiny Meadow also acknowledged the difficulty of dealing with bottles at the end of their useful life. Lin Rong, the brand’s director, said the company had already been using recyclable packaging materials but that there was still a gap when it came to bottles that recycling companies regarded as low-value plastic. “We are pleased to have found a meaningful use for our empty bottles,” Lin said, describing the road project as a way of giving the packaging a more circular journey.Dow turned plastic waste into road materialDow's solution collects the hard-to-recycle plastic and turns it into post-consumer recycled plastic for polymer-modified asphalt. The recycled material was then incorporated into the road paving process, turning thousands of unwanted bottles into part of the infrastructure at ECUST's Xuhui Campus. In total, more than 6,000 used milk bottles and other plastic waste went into the project.The project was also presented as an example of how materials science could create new uses for plastic that traditional recycling systems struggled to handle. Bambang Candra, Dow’s Asia Pacific commercial vice president for Packaging & Speciality Plastics, said, “Using our materials science expertise, we help bring a new purpose to waste bottles.” He added that the company hoped the project would encourage other brand owners to find ways of reducing plastic waste.How the plastic road could cut emissionsThe project was intended to do more than simply dispose of unwanted plastic in a different form. Dow said keeping the waste out of the environment, reducing the amount of bitumen required and potentially extending the service life of roads could also reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and energy consumption. The company therefore presented the road as an example of turning a waste problem into an infrastructure application.For Shiny Meadow, the project fitted into a broader idea of circularity. Lin Rong said the company wanted its plastic packaging to have “a circular journey” rather than follow a traditional take-make-use path. The road offered one possible destination for plastic bottles that had little value to conventional recyclers, giving the discarded packaging a practical use after its original purpose had ended.Dow’s recycled plastic road projects across AsiaThe Shanghai project was part of Dow’s wider work on using recycled plastic in roads across Asia. The company said it had begun improving roads with recycled plastic in Depok City, Indonesia, in 2017. It later worked with partners in India on roads in Pune and Bangalore and had begun a collaboration with Siam Cement Group in Thailand.ECUST viewed the Shanghai road as a practical demonstration of how unconventional approaches could be used to tackle plastic waste. Professor Li Tao, the university’s vice president, said the institution hoped the collaboration would inspire students to explore unusual sustainability solutions and apply creative ideas on a larger scale.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 8 Best Gluten-Free Meal Delivery Services to Try in 2026
articles.summary: Find some of the best meal delivery services with gluten-free options. Get gluten-free meal kits from Sunbasket, Splendid Spoon, Hungryroot, Purple Carrot and more.
articles.body: Meal kit delivery services have plenty of benefits: They can be a great way to prepare fun and flavorful meals without having to sprint to the grocery store each week. But when it comes to specific dietary restrictions like a gluten-free diet — which limits the intake of wheat, barley and several other grains — it can be hard to pinpoint ones that fit your needs. Fortunately, many meal kits and pre-made meal delivery services offer gluten-free menu items and plans for tasty, creative and easy-to-prepare meals when you’re in a rush. To determine the best meal delivery services with gluten-free options or entirely gluten-free menus, I spoke to nutritionists and dietitians about the best services to try out and highlighted each individual service’s pricing, delivery frequency and meal options. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Best gluten-free meal delivery services I spoke to experts about their favorite meal delivery services that either provide gluten-free options or have an entirely gluten-free menu. I highlighted their specific recommendations below — all of which offer pre-made meals or a combination of meal kits and ready-made items — and noted their costs, serving sizes, and the number of meals they deliver per week. Best overall Sunbasket offers both ingredient-based meal kits and pre-made meals, all of which the brand says consist of high-quality ingredients and organic produce. One of Sunbasket’s 10 available meal plans is the Gluten-Free Friendly meal plan, which has five to eight gluten-free options each week. NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin, who follows a pescatarian and gluten-free diet, tried Sunbasket for a week and loved the service’s variety of meals and delicious pre-made options. “The particular recipes I chose forced me to use ingredients that aren’t in my regular rotation, like turmeric and artichoke dip, and make foods that aren’t typically top of mind for me, like potato salad,” says Malin. Both Ariane Resnick, a special diet chef and certified nutritionist, and Lisa Moskovitz, CEO of NY Nutrition Group, say Sunbasket is their top choice for healthy meal kit deliveries. “It has a variety of options that can be modified for carnivores and strictly plant-based eaters alike,” says Moskovitz. The Fresh & Ready option, which comes with single-serve meals you can heat in the oven or microwave in just a few minutes, also has several gluten-free options to choose from. If you don’t feel like committing to a single plan, the service lets you mix and match with over a dozen meals from its weekly rotating menu. Best health-conscious Splendid Spoon has over 50 healthy, ready-made meals and snacks that include smoothies, soups, noodle bowls and larger dishes— and everything is gluten-free. You can select a box size of seven, 14 or 21 meals and choose your meals for the week. Your cart will automatically fill with Splendid Spoon’s bestsellers, or you can manually swap in your favorites. Resnick recommends the service for anyone who wants healthy meals in a flash. “They taste as healthy as they are, which is a downside for some and a bonus for others.” she says. The large selection of juices and smoothies and the convenience of thawing one at a time is also a big plus, says Resnick. Best budget-friendly Purple Carrot offers both prepared meals and meal kits, so you can choose the level of effort that you want to put into your meals. The meals are all fully plant-based, and Purple Carrot provides several gluten-free recipes to choose from, as well as gluten-free pre-prepared meals. “The meal kits are a wonderful blend of familiar and innovative — think kimchi grilled cheese and Baklava overnight oats,” says Resnick. And because the meals are fully plant-based, Purple Carrot can be an easy way for people to “add more plant foods into their diets without having to fully convert to veganism,” she says. You can customize the number of dinners you get per week, which range from two to four meal kits and six to 10 pre-made meals. Deliveries take place on Mondays, Tuesdays or Wednesdays depending on your shipping location, and you can choose to skip a delivery on any given week. Best for beginners Epicured allows you to choose from a rotating menu of over 50 pre-made meals spanning breakfast, lunch, dinner, snacks and desserts. All Epicured meals are entirely gluten-free and low-FODMAP, which means they don’t feature certain carbohydrates and food additives that can be hard for some people to digest. “They’re a great option for those with SIBO, IBS or a generally sensitive tummy,” says Moskovitz. If you don’t want to choose individual meals, Epicured also offers several pre-selected programs, including an omnivore, pescetarian and vegetarian program, that helps you ease into a low-FODMAP diet, according to the brand. Once you select your meals and register, each weekly order is automatically renewed — if you don’t manually pick your meals, orders are locked in on Friday afternoons with the same meals you previously selected. Best chef-prepared Having a gluten-free diet doesn’t mean you need to sacrifice the joys of dining out. Cookunity offers chef-prepared meals with a wide range of gluten-free options for you to enjoy at home, with subscriptions ranging from four to 16 meals per week, Resnick says this service is one of her favorites: “I appreciate that they provide full ingredient lists, down to the individual ingredients in cheeses.” Former NBC Selected social commerce editor Sadhana Daruvuri also enjoys it because she can get a variety of delicious meals while still spending about the same amount she’d spent on groceries, she says. You can also filter meals by other dietary restrictions, like dairy-free, high protein, vegan, vegetarian and more. Best for multiple dietary restrictions BistroMD offers a specialized gluten-free plan that lets you choose from over 100 gluten-free meals each week, according to the service. The Gluten-Free program provides breakfast, lunch and dinner for your choice of five days or seven days. The service also offers an EATS (Essential and Tasty Snacks) program that provides healthy snacking options for an additional charge. “ BistroMD prides itself on being ‘doctor-designed’ and therefore is more medically therapeutic than most other companies,” says Moskovitz. Best splurge-worthy Although Sakara is on the pricier side for a meal delivery service, it offers a large selection of ready-to-eat meals, all of which are gluten-free, organic, dairy-free and plant-based, according to the service. articles.title: Declassified CIA documents show clear warnings to presidents before 9/11
articles.summary: Newly declassified documents show the CIA repeatedly warned Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush that Osama bin Laden was determined to strike at the United States, as far back as three years before the 9/11 attacks.
articles.body: Newly declassified documents show the CIA repeatedly warned Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush that Osama bin Laden was determined to strike at the United States, as far back as three years before the 9/11 attacks. The high-level warnings lacked definitive information about precisely how or when the attacks might take place. But one intelligence report to the president in September 1998 came tantalizingly close to grasping what might be coming, stating that bin Laden’s supporters “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city.” The same memo states that “intelligence provides no conclusive information on bin Ladin’s intentions for future attacks.” The document was one of dozens of formerly top-secret presidential briefings related to the 9/11 attacks released by the CIA on Friday, the 25th anniversary of deadly Al Qaeda terror attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people. The documents, posted on the CIA’s website, cover the period from February 1998 to Sept. 12, 2001. All are drawn from the daily intelligence briefings that were given by the CIA and other spy agencies to Clinton and his successor, Bush. In a statement, CIA Director John Ratcliffe called it “the single largest release of CIA analysis related to 9/11 ever.” “Americans can now see for themselves the intelligence leading up to this tragic day for our Nation,” Ratcliffe said in a post on X. The documents, which amount to more than 100 pages, show a steady stream of alarming but imprecise intelligence reports that bin Laden was preparing to attack the United States, either on U.S. soil or at embassies and U.S. military bases abroad. Many of them were heavily redacted. But the documents included no major new revelations, as previous inquiries by Congress and accounts by officials in government at the time had made clear that the intelligence agencies were aware of the growing threat from Al Qaeda. The September 1998 intelligence briefing about the possibility of using an explosive-laden plane to target an American city was written only weeks after bin Laden’s supporters bombed U.S. embassies in East Africa and after a failed attempt by the Clinton administration to kill the Al Qaeda leader with Tomahawk missile strikes in Afghanistan and Sudan. After the failed missile strikes on Aug. 20, 1998, an intelligence brief eight days later to the president concluded that bin Laden and other terrorist leaders based in Afghanistan “survived the US strikes and their communications network remains intact” and that training for militants had resumed at some camps. Other intelligence memos stated that bin Laden’s militants were training to hijack commercial airliners, experimenting with crude chemical or other unconventional weapons, doing dry runs to test U.S. airport security, plotting to take hostages and trafficking narcotics to fund terrorism plans. The intelligence reports to the White House also consistently found that bin Laden was in no danger of being expelled by the Taliban regime in Afghanistan, even though some senior figures worried his plotting against the U.S. could put the Taliban in jeopardy. The “Taliban is not likely to give up bin Ladin for less than full diplomatic recognition and significant reconstruction aid,” said one intelligence memo from March 26, 2001. By Aug. 6, 2001, the intelligence community provided yet another bleak assessment to the president, titled: “bin Ladin determined to strike in US.” “Clandestine, foreign government, and media reports indicate bin Ladin since 1997 has wanted to conduct terrorist attacks in the US,” the briefing states. The document drop came the same day that 9/11 widow Terry Strada broke with the long-standing tradition of keeping politics out of Sept. 11 remembrances and called on President Donald Trump to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for the attacks. “Tell the Saudis to stop lying,” said Strada, who lost her husband, Tom, during the attacks and raised their three children on her own. “Tell them if they want to be friends with the USA they cannot continue to deny all of this — all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through.” Trump was at the memorial ceremony at the Pentagon, but Vice President JD Vance was in lower Manhattan. So Strada directed her message at him. “Vice President Vance, thank you for being here today. Please carry that message back, stand with the families, stand with the survivors, stand with Americans, as my husband Tom said that is always the right thing to do,” Strada said. Fifteen of the Al Qaeda plane hijackers were Saudi nationals. And Strada is part of a coalition of 9/11 families that believes the Saudis were complicit in the attacks and has sued the country’s government. The Saudis deny that claim and are fighting the lawsuit in court. Strada, who is seeking information about two Saudi nationals in California the FBI gathered as part of “Operation Encore,” told NBC News last year that “because of this lawsuit we now know there was critical evidence in the hands of the FBI within days of the attacks.” “It was never properly analyzed or shared with the 9/11 Commission,” Strada said. The 9/11 Commission was an independent, bipartisan group created to investigate the Sept. 11 attacks. It concluded in a report released in 2004 that poor communication between the FBI and the CIA, a failure to “connect the dots” of intelligence about Al Qaeda suspects, as well as a “failure of imagination” within the U.S. national security apparatus, enabled the terrorists to pierce America’s defenses. The report led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

articles.title: Houthi advance in Yemen is about more than just the Red Sea
articles.summary: Houthis were already able to disrupt shipping – their advance consolidates that power, and exposes government weakness.
articles.body:
The rapid Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week is an astonishing military victory, but not quite the game-changer it is being portrayed as.

The group has been able to threaten the vitally important shipping route , but they have been doing so since 2023. This new victory consolidates that control, proving that Yemen’s government is not currently in a position to defeat them.

The prior Houthi control over the northern section of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, including the major port city of Hodeidah, has allowed the Iran-allied rebel group, for years, to first attack shipping linked to Israel and the United States – and then, in recent months, Saudi Arabian-linked vessels .

That control also damaged the global economy. Long before the US war with Iran and the transformation of the Strait of Hormuz into a tool to throttle international trade, Houthi attacks around Yemen had turned Bab al-Mandeb into a similar weapon, and led to bombing campaigns against the Houthis by the US, the United Kingdom, and Israel.

Houthi officials themselves have emphasised this, with one leading official, Abdulqader al-Murtada, saying earlier this week that the group did “not need control over Bab al-Mandeb, for the blockade [on Saudi ships] is already in place”. Al-Murtada could point Saudi ships that have avoided Bab al-Mandeb since the Houthis began attacking them in July, even before their latest progress.

However, the Houthi lightning advance makes it even easier for the group to disrupt shipping. They now have access to the Red Sea’s narrow entry point and several islands in it, allowing them to use shorter-range weapons and more easily reach vessels they want to attack and board, as well as potentially using sea mines to further restrict shipping.

The increase in the Houthi ability to target shipping – even with the caveats outlined above – does have an impact on market sentiment. Oil prices have increased as traders price in the ability for Iran and its allies to disrupt shipping in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, the two maritime chokepoints of the southern Arabian Peninsula.

However, the consequences of this advance are not limited to the increased ability of the Houthis to attack shipping, but to the increasing reality that the Houthi problem on the Red Sea is not going away.

For months, after Saudi Arabia backed a Yemeni government campaign against southern Yemeni separatist forces earlier this year, the mood had shifted in the country’s anti-Houthi camp.

The perception was that the Yemeni government, led by the Presidential Leadership Council, had finally gotten its act together. President Rashad al-Alimi repeatedly spoke of a unified military chain of command, allowing the military to overcome the divisions blamed for its inability to defeat the Houthis.

Yemeni and Saudi officials had hinted at an anti-Houthi campaign all year. The Red Sea coastline was a possible location: the largely flat geography suited the government, allowing Saudi Arabia to effectively use its air power; much of the population is not made up of the Houthis’ traditional support base; and prior Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping meant that there would likely be international buy-in for such a campaign.

The seizure of the Red Sea coastline has broken all of those narratives.

The momentum the Yemeni government thought it had, even at the start of this week when it claimed advances in al-Jawf, to the east of the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, is now gone.

After months of projecting unity, Yemen’s anti-Houthi camp is once again turning on itself, trading accusations of blame for the defeat.

The message the Houthis have for Saudi Arabia is clear: ‘Your partners in Yemen can’t defeat us.’

Therefore, the potential Houthi argument is that Saudi Arabia has to make a deal with them and agree to their terms, including Riyadh funding public sector salaries, access to income from Yemen’s oil and gas reserves, and no restrictions on flights and shipping to Houthi-controlled ports.

The Houthis have an incentive to lock in their gains and raise the cost of escalation before Saudi-backed Yemeni forces can reorganise.

Their attacks on Saudi Arabia, escalating in the past week, have been damaging, and the group is promising more if Riyadh increases its military support for the Yemeni government.

The risk of any such intervention is clearly there for Saudi Arabia. But so is the risk of inaction. The Houthis have repeatedly demanded more concessions when they were in positions of strength.

With the Yemen war unresolved, the Houthis may decide to escalate again in the future, even if a deal is agreed now.

And so, policymakers in Riyadh could determine that it makes more sense to make a concerted effort to deal with the problem head-on now, rather than allow it to fester into the future.

articles.body: Princess Alexandra of Hanover, the granddaughter of Hollywood legend Grace Kelly and daughter of Princess Caroline of Monaco, is engaged to her longtime boyfriend Ben-Sylvester Strautmann after nearly a decade together.Alexandra, 27, announced her engagement on Friday, sharing photographs with Strautmann on Instagram. The couple have been together since their teenage years and have maintained a relatively private relationship despite their connection to Monaco's royal family.Alexandra is the youngest child of Princess Caroline of Monaco and her third husband, Ernst August, Prince of Hanover. She is also the niece of Monaco's reigning monarch, Prince Albert II.For those familiar with Monaco's royal family, Alexandra is part of the next generation of a dynasty that has long attracted global attention. Her grandmother was Grace Kelly, the American film star who married Monaco's Prince Rainier III in 1956 and became Princess Grace of Monaco.Alexandra was born in Austria and grew up between Monaco and other parts of Europe. She studied history and literature in Paris and has also been involved in figure skating. As a member of Monaco's extended royal family, she regularly appears at major events in the principality and has attended fashion shows and high-profile social occasions.Who is Ben-Sylvester Strautmann?Unlike his fiancée, Strautmann is not a member of a royal family. The 27-year-old German has largely kept a low profile despite dating Alexandra for almost 10 years.He grew up in Monaco after moving there with his family as a child and has a background in business. He was also a competitive basketball player in his younger years.Strautmann comes from a wealthy German family with business interests, but he has generally stayed away from the spotlight surrounding Monaco's royals.His relationship with Alexandra first became public around 2017, when the pair were still teenagers. Since then, they have increasingly been seen together at events connected to Monaco's royal and social circles.The couple have attended the Monaco Grand Prix, the Monte-Carlo Masters and the principality's famous Rose Ball together. Despite their high-profile surroundings, they have largely avoided turning their relationship into a public spectacle.A royal romance that lasted a decadeAlexandra and Strautmann's relationship has stood out partly because of its longevity. They have been together through Alexandra's university years and into adulthood, while continuing to make occasional appearances together at major events.Their engagement now adds another royal wedding to the European social calendar.For Alexandra, the marriage will mark a new chapter for a royal who occupies a unique place in Monaco's family tree — the granddaughter of Grace Kelly, daughter of Princess Caroline and niece of Prince Albert II.The couple has yet to announce details of their wedding date or venue.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
articles.summary: The capture by the rebels of a stretch Yemen's strategic coastline is the group's most impressive military coup for several years.
articles.body:
The Houthis' lightning advance across the southern reaches of the Tihamah – Yemen's arid coastal plain – appears to have taken most observers by surprise.

Until recently, the anti-Houthi coalition known as the National Resistance held significant territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast. In a matter of days, much of this has fallen to the Houthis.

According to some estimates, the Iranian-backed rebels have captured as much as 130km (81 miles) of the country's strategically important coastline.

It's the group's most impressive military coup for several years, proving that despite a civil war that has lasted 12 years, devastating Saudi air raids and attacks by American, Israeli and British forces, the Houthis remain a force to be reckoned with.

With their opponents stunned and demoralised, it's unlikely the Houthis will be dislodged any time soon.

Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane

Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes

"Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."

Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" – Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.

"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."

Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.

Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).

"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."

"This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.

If the Houthis have also taken control of several key islands in the Red Sea, including Perim - which sits in the middle of the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab - then the group's ability to interfere with international shipping will be greatly enhanced.

As the group's actions in the wake of Israel's war on Gaza proved, shipping in the Red Sea is highly vulnerable to Houthi missiles, drones and small attack boats.

"They were able to control what was going in and out of the Bab al-Mandab and up towards Suez without having these territorial gains," Yemen expert Iona Craig told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"But of course now they're controlling the area immediately overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, and this gives them far more leverage."

Shipping companies are likely to be sceptical about the sincerity of a statement released on Friday afternoon, in which the Houthi military said that maritime navigation was "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels, which have already been subject to a blockade".

In their earlier attacks, the Houthis said they were only targeting vessels linked to Israel, but in fact hit ships with no such connection, including a Norwegian-flagged tanker.

Craig said the Houthis may nevertheless refrain from indiscriminate attacks, fearing a repeat of Operation Rough Rider - six weeks of major US air and naval strikes in the spring of 2025.

"They've already felt the wrath of the US," she said.

But would the US want to get involved anyway?

President Donald Trump's war with Iran is already unpopular. With oil prices creeping back up, it's doubtful that a new front would do much to enhance his approval ratings or his Republican party's chances in November's midterm US elections.

According to the Axios website, appeals for US intervention from the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have so far gone unanswered.

Axios writes that the US "is increasingly concerned about the escalating conflict in Yemen and is working to intensify its support for the kingdom while simultaneously seeking to avoid direct military involvement".

But it's not just the potential threat to the Bab al-Mandab that's causing fear in Saudi Arabia.

Satellite images of an apparent Houthi missile-and-drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline – a vital alternative route for oil exports following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year – point to an effort by Iran's Yemeni allies to add to the economic pressures generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Even if Iran did not directly order the attack, it clearly stands to benefit.

Baraa Shaiban, a researcher and analyst at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, says the origins of the latest upsurge in fighting – the worst since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 - can be traced back to July, when a Houthi delegation returned from the state funeral of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

"Immediately after, the escalation started," he says, "and it looked very clearly that [Iran was] determined to now have a bigger foothold on the Red Sea".

With Yemen teetering on the edge of a return to all-out war, Saudi Arabia anxious about preserving its economic lifeline to the Red Sea and Donald Trump apparently reluctant to get involved, America's conflict with Iran just took on a new and potentially dangerous dimension.

For the people of Yemen, displaced, bombed, starved and impoverished by a dozen years of civil war, recent developments can only make their lives worse.

articles.title: A New York jeweler has been released from prison in Iran but is banned from leaving war-torn country
articles.summary: NEW YORK — An Iranian American jeweler from New York has been released from prison in Iran, but he is prohibited from leaving the country, according to his family and federal officials.
articles.body: NEW YORK — An Iranian American jeweler from New York has been released from prison in Iran, but he is prohibited from leaving the country, according to his family and federal officials. Kamran Hekmati was let out of Tehran’s notorious Evin prison on Sept. 5 after completing about half of a two-year sentence, his family recently wrote on a website advocating for his release. The family said they are also “desperately afraid for his health and well-being” as he requires regular medical checkups to ensure his bladder cancer doesn’t relapse. “The Iranian regime couldn’t care less,” the family wrote of Hekmati’s medical challenges. “Much like other wrongful detention cases in Iran, Kamran appears to be caught up in Iran’s traditional approach of detaining Americans to obtain political concessions from the US.” Representatives for the family and the federal government didn’t say where Hekmati, 62, is currently staying in Iran or how many other Americans are currently believed detained in the country. Shohreh Nowfar, Hekmati’s cousin in California, said Friday that the family are “excited” and hopeful his passport can be returned soon so he can leave the country, which has been at war with the U.S. and Israel for more than six months now. “We continue to hope this is a signal from the Iranian side as to their willingness to send Kamran home,” added Kieran Ramsey, chief investigative officer at Global Reach, a U.S. nonprofit working on Hekmati’s case. The Iranian American, who is also Jewish, owns a jewelry business in Manhattan’s Diamond District and has lived with his family for years in Great Neck Estates, on suburban Long Island. He was arrested by Iranian authorities last July after having his passport seized while trying to fly out of the airport in Tehran that May. Hekmati’s family says he was charged under an Iranian law that bans Iranian citizens from visiting Israel within the last 10 years. But they maintain his last trip to Israel was 13 years ago -- prior to the passage of the law -- for his son’s bar mitzvah. “Mr. Hekmati did nothing wrong,” said U.S. Rep. Thomas Suozzi, a Long Island Democrat who advocated for the State Department to officially designate Hekmati as wrongfully detained earlier this year. “We cannot rest until he is reunited with his family.” The State Department similarly called on Iran to lift its so-called exit ban so Hekmati can return to the U.S. It also said the country should “immediately release” Iranian American journalist Reza Valizadeh and other Americans “unjustly detained in Iran.” Representatives for Valizadeh didn’t immediately return emails seeking comment Friday. But in recent months, he has sent voice messages from prison describing conditions inside Evin prison, a high-security facility that holds many of the Islamic Republic’s political prisoners. In an August recording, Valizadeh, who has been imprisoned since 2024, said prison officials have not allowed his family to visit for the past five months. He also said medical care is “almost non-existent” save for the most basic medications. “Diseases that were eradicated decades ago have returned inside the prison, including pulmonary and gastrointestinal tuberculosis,” he said in the voice message, which was shared by CBS. Valizadeh also said that prior to his release, Hekmati had been granted a medical furlough for cancer treatment but was ordered back to prison after about a month, rather than being allowed to begin chemotherapy. Like Hekmati, Valizadeh has also been officially designated wrongfully detained by the U.S. government. He was arrested after returning to Iran to visit his elderly parents and charged with collaborating with the U.S. government. Valizadeh obtained U.S. citizenship in 2022 while working in Washington, D.C., for Radio Farda, the Persian-language arm of Radio Free Europe, which receives U.S. government funding. He is among at leas nine reporters currently jailed in Iran, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.

articles.title: Gayle King stunned after learning dissenting Clancy trial juror was a Black man
articles.summary: Co-host Gayle King was visibly stunned on "CBS Mornings" after learning the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial was reportedly a Black man.
articles.body: "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King was stunned after learning that the lone dissenting juror in the Lindsay Clancy trial was purportedly a Black man during a Friday interview. Paula Devlin, one of the jurors who was part of the 11-person majority in favor of finding Clancy not criminally responsible for strangling her three young children, explained that the lone holdout was a Black man and the only person of color on the jury in an interview with King on the network morning show. "Whoa. I have to sit with that for just a second," said King, who appeared visibly flustered by the revelation. LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR WHO BACKED THE DEFENSE ALSO PUBLICLY CHEERED KAREN READ'S ACQUITTAL Devlin also said ages among the jurors ranged between 22 and "70-ish." Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial last week after jurors could not agree on a verdict. They told the court they were split 11-1, with the lone male holdout being the only one voting to convict Clancy of first-degree murder for the deaths of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. A fellow juror, Nick Dargie, 25, told ABC News that the lone holdout juror at one point attempted to mimic the way Clancy killed her three kids with an exercise band and water bottle. "He took the exercise band out of the bag, grabbed an empty water bottle and tied the band around the water bottle and pulled it," Dargie said. "I was just so shocked that he did that." "I was shocked, it didn't make any sense to me. Like, we're not in here to play detective or it's not a game of Clue. Like, this is serious. I asked him why," he added. LINDSAY CLANCY JURY RECAP: DAY 5 ENDS WITH NO VERDICT AFTER RARE INSTRUCTION Dargie said the holdout juror refused to explain how witness testimony helped prove his stance. "There was several times I would ask him to show us evidence or, you know, describe a witness testimony that helped to prove what he was saying, and ... he couldn't," Dargie said. "There wasn't a single piece of evidence or witness testimony that he used to prove why he was thinking the way he was, which is why we ultimately sent in that note." Dargie was referring to the note sent by the jury foreperson, who reported that one juror was refusing to follow the court's instructions on reasonable doubt. Curtis Houck, the Managing Editor of the NewsBusters division of the Media Research Center, a media watchdog group, helped the clip go viral by sharing it in a social media post and summarizing the exchange. He later spoke to Fox News Digital about the clip, arguing the host's surprise was one of many responses from media figures that speak volumes about American culture. "The woke women propping up these 11 jurors and either directly or indirectly smearing this holdout juror have had their lives completely upended by this stunning declaration. King — whose best friend Oprah recently taped a sympathetic, pro-Clancy special — came off as though she had just been hit by a proverbial bus, meaning she clearly thought he was a White male she could stereotype," he said. "The fact that she further pressed for information about his age showed the dangers this holdout juror is facing, now that he has been identified by gender, race, and a rough age," Houck added. "King will now be known by many for this cartoonish reaction." articles.title: Tragic death of woman who testified against father in notorious mafia murder of mother
articles.summary: Denise Cosco testified against the powerful 'Ndrangheta clan and her own father over the murder of her mother in Italy.
articles.body:
A woman who testified against her own father after her mother was murdered in a notorious mafia killing in Italy is believed to have taken her own life.

Denise Cosco was found critically injured on Sunday and died later in hospital in Rome.

Her mother Lea Garofalo, who was killed in 2009, became a powerful symbol of resistance to the mafia after turning witness for the state against the 'Ndrangheta clan in southern Italy.

Those close to Cosco recall her bravery in speaking out at her father's trial, but also her tremendous struggle in the years that followed.

At 35, she died at the same age her mother was when she was murdered.

Enza Rando, a senator and anti-mafia lawyer who represented Cosco at the murder trial, described her death as "a profound wound for the entire country", and proof that the mafia not only kills, but creates "true monsters in the lives and souls" of those who survive.

Francesca Rispoli, co-president of the anti-mafia organisation Libera, said the death highlighted the struggle experienced by many who break with organised crime.

"The mafia, it's not just something physical. You can leave. You can change your name," she told the BBC. "But there is still a tie, a family tie, that stays… deep inside and is impossible to overcome."

Cosco, like her mother, had lived under state protection with a new name and identity for many years.

But Rispoli said she remained extremely vulnerable and had reconnected with her father, Carlo Cosco, in prison in recent years because, despite everything, she had felt a "hole in her life".

Friends say she struggled with mental health problems and addiction.

"Maybe this is a sign that those trying to lead another life need more support. Not just for one year – maybe their whole life," Rispoli argued, as organised crime groups in Italy – especially the 'Ndrangheta - involve close-knit family networks.

In Cosco's case, both her mother's family and her father were tied to the mafia.

She had always refused to believe her father's story that her mother had abandoned her to start a new life in Australia.

In fact, he had tricked Garofalo to a meeting, then had her strangled, her body dismembered then incinerated.

Several years later, a statement by one of the killers finally allowed police to recover some fragments of bone and a necklace, which Cosco identified.

At a public funeral in 2013, she spoke of her mother's courage in "putting herself on the line… for justice for all".

Her father and three accomplices were already serving life in prison.

At the trial, Cosco described herself as a "proud witness for justice" and said she had taken the difficult choice to testify – speaking from behind a screen – because she wanted "inner freedom to start over" with her life.

Prosecutors have now opened an investigation to determine whether there was any incitement to suicide and her phone has been seized for analysis.

Friends and supporters were due to gather in Milan on Friday evening to remember her near the spot where her mother was abducted.

"Denise's entire life revolved between the two extremes of courage and suffering," Luigi Ciotti, president of Libera wrote, calling that a difficult balance.

"Today, something in that fragile equilibrium was broken forever."

articles.title: Indian-origin investor's H-1B prediction: If 10% of Indians stuck in US Green Card backlog return, India’s GDP could rise 1%
articles.summary: US News: Indian-American entrepreneur Vivek Wadhwa said if Indians waiting for residency in the US go back to India as America First activists want them to, it.
articles.body: Indian-American entrepreneur Vivek Wadhwa said if Indians waiting for residency in the US go back to India as America First activists want them to, it will be India's gain. India could get a major economic boost if skilled Indians caught in the US green-card backlog begin returning home, Wadhwa predicted, arguing that the return of even a fraction of them could add 1% to India's GDP over the next two to three years.Wadhwa made the prediction in a post on X while discussing the growing debate over H-1B visas and the possibility of skilled Indian workers leaving the US amid tightening immigration policies. The US administration moved towards eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders in the latest move. If this proposal becomes a rule, then H-1B visa holders and their family members will be out of legal status in the US the day the H-1B visa holder loses their job. Now, H-1B visa holders get 60 days to plan for the future after layoff but in the new proposal, the last day in the job would also be the last day in the US.“With all the debates about H-1Bs and sending skilled Indians back, here’s my prediction: this could add 1% to India’s GDP over the next 2–3 years alone,” Wadhwa wrote.Wadhwa said more than one million Indians are stuck in America's green-card backlog. If just 10% of them return to India, he estimates that would mean around 100,000 highly skilled workers coming back with their savings, professional experience and networks.“Imagine if 20% or 30% returned,” he wrote, suggesting the economic impact could be considerably larger.Wadhwa's argument is that a reversal of that migration could give India access not only to skilled workers but also to people who have spent years building careers in the US and accumulated capital, business connections and knowledge of the American market.“The flow is already in reverse,” Wadhwa wrote, describing the potential movement of Indian professionals back to their home country as a possible turning point.He argued that India could turn what is being viewed as a setback for Indian immigrants in the US into an economic opportunity. “America's loss could become India's biggest economic gain,” he wrote.H-1B debate adds to uncertaintyWadhwa's comments come as the US immigration system faces renewed debate over H-1B visas and employment-based immigration.He has previously called for the H-1B programme to be scrapped and replaced with a new skilled-immigration system, arguing that the programme has been undermined by labour arbitrage, so-called body shops and long green-card backlogs.In August, Wadhwa argued that the US should move away from a system that leaves skilled immigrants dependent on employers and instead create an immigration framework that gives talented workers greater freedom to change jobs and launch companies.His latest post takes that argument a step further, suggesting that restrictions and uncertainty in the US could accelerate a reverse brain drain, with experienced Indian professionals choosing to build their careers and businesses in India.But will these Indians return?Many social media users argued that Wadhwa's premise is wrong, as Indians stuck in the US GreeCard queue would prefer to explore European countries instead of going back to India. "It’s a mistaken belief. Who would come here with taxes so high , poor water and air quality and C grade civic infrastructure. I have engaged with lot of them and they all are planning to shift to some European country / Canada / Australia," one wrote.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: NMC adds over 13,000 MBBS seats, total intake tops 1.4 lakh
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has approved 13,186 additional MBBS seats for the 2026-27 academic year, taking the total approved un.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has approved 13,186 additional MBBS seats for the 2026-27 academic year, taking the total approved undergraduate medical intake to 1,40,214 seats across 836 medical colleges, excluding seats at the Institutes of National Importance (INIs).The updated seat matrix, as on September 1, incorporates permissions for new medical colleges and increases in the annual intake of existing medical colleges.The expansion comes as NEET-UG counselling for the 2026-27 MBBS batch is under way, with the counselling schedule pushing back the start of the academic session and subsequent rounds, including the stray vacancy round, expected to continue into Oct.The increase is heavily driven by the private sector, which accounts for 10,400 of the 13,186 additional seats, or nearly 79%, while govt medical colleges have added 2,786 seats. The total intake has risen from 1,27,028 renewed seats to 1,40,214, an increase of about 10.4%.Karnataka has recorded the highest increase with 1,650 additional seats; followed by Tamil Nadu with 1,250; Bihar with 1,240; Uttar Pradesh with 1,200 and Rajasthan with 1,100. Telangana has added 1,010 seats and West Bengal 975.Karnataka's total MBBS intake now stands at 15,745 seats, including 4,600 in govt colleges and 11,145 in private colleges. Tamil Nadu has 14,299 seats, Uttar Pradesh 14,400 and Maharashtra 13,249. The addition of 13,186 seats will widen the pool of MBBS seats available during the 2026-27 admission cycle, although the actual allocation of these seats will depend on the ongoing counselling process.Among other major increases, Andhra Pradesh has added 525 seats, Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand 520 each, Maharashtra 550, Haryana 350, Kerala 300, Gujarat 250, Puducherry and Uttarakhand 200 each, and Jammu and Kashmir 175.The NMC matrix shows zero increase in Delhi, while Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Dadra and Nagar Haveli have also recorded no additional seats.The NMC has made it clear that admissions must be restricted to the number of seats approved in the matrix, with admissions beyond the approved intake liable to regulatory action.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
